speechtext: Not with me.

-to lengthen the hours of sittings with the hope that this would be one measure to expedite the work of the house. During the progress of these discussions the hon. member for Fraser Valley talked to me about them and informed me what was being discussed, as I presume the house leaders of the other parties did with their leader. We agreed with the government house leader that we would support such recommendation; and we give our support to it now without anymore discussion.
I do not believe this is the only answer to speeding up the work of the house but it is one measure, at least of intent and good will on the part of the parties in this house to do something better than what we have been doing. Therefore, while we are all concerned about a summer recess, we are also concerned about priorities and about making more progress, so let us agree with the proposal that has been put before us by the government house leader.

Mr. Speaker, we support the motion presented by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) concerning the extension of the sitting hours in order that we can have a summer recess.

I heard a while ago the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) tell us that we should defer the debate on the flag issue to deal with exports, family allowances, the labour code, etc. It is true that exports, in short, any problem concerning the national economy is more important than the adoption of a flag. However, we do not object to accepting immediately a distinctive national flag. If the Leader of the Opposition were ready to vote today on the resolution for a distinctive national flag, this would settle the problem, because every Canadian wants one.
As for part (b) of the resolution, we could wait till next fall or the spring to discuss it. However, it is surely not the flag issue which prevents the government at present from legislating or from introducing its legislation. It is the opposition that wants to discuss the flag to submit its own design in an attempt to confuse the issue as much as possible.
Let us put a stop to our discussion and settle the matter of the flag right now. As I said yesterday, and I repeat it today, the cleavage between the two racial groups of Canada is getting even worse, and I hold the Leader of the Opposition responsible for this situation.
Mr. Speaker, we, in this part of the house, are ready to vote on the flag resolution immediately and to proceed afterwards with the legislation to see what can be done as soon as possible.
We strongly and fully support the motion of the Minister of Justice, leader of the house, to extend the hours so as to enable us to pass some pieces of legislation which will prove beneficial, we hope, to the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I believe there was agreement, certainly in my party, to an extension of hours if that is going to accomplish something. But I wonder whether the general public is not asking itself what we are really concerned to pass, and whether there will be a recess or whether we intend to go on throughout the summer. The Prime Minister, in a genial, offhand way, said we might have a long week end some time in September. If that is the case I see no reason to consider any changes in the order covering our sitting hours. The public must wonder just what are the legislative preferences of the Prime Minister. I can only think of three things which need to be passed before a recess, if the Prime Minister wants a recess in July. They are, of course, family allowances, student loans
Business of the House
and interim supply. If the government wanted interim supply for the next three months they should have asked for it, instead of asking for only one month's supply. The Prime Minister shrugs his shoulders. I am sure he is aware that if he gets interim supply now he has immediately to begin considering next month's supply. The right hon. gentleman can shrug his shoulders and laugh about it if he wants to, but he must be aware of these things, or if not he should be.
A great deal has been said about getting on with the business of the house, but how can one really arrange things when the leader of the government is not willing to say what he wants? The last time he spoke on this subject in the house he read a long list of items he wanted us to pass, a list containing some 35 or 37 items. Some of those things have been on the order paper for a couple of years. Surely he was not serious about that list. Some of these things have been around for a long time.
Too long.

I think it is silly to tell the public we intend to accomplish something by extending our hours as an emergency measure. I am inclined to agree with the Leader of the Opposition when he says "Let us change the rules, lengthen the hours and make it a permanent arrangement". As for asking the house to make exceptions, to change the rules for the purpose of obtaining a summer recess, the Prime Minister will have to be more honest with the house than he has previously been.
I do not really care if we start the business of the house at nine o'clock in the morning and run it through to twelve o'clock at night. It does not matter to me, but let us adhere to it all the time. This is not an emergency; this situation has been cropping up throughout the seven years I have been in the house. It is not only the present Prime Minister who is concerned; the previous prime minister was in exactly the same position. We have no timetable here. We do not know what we are going to do at a certain time or when we are going to complete it.
The backbenchers in this house have some responsibility, too, and they should know what they are going to do. They should know what it is intended to place on the order paper and what is the government's preference for legislation. If the government wants to go on with the flag issue it may cake a couple of months-

Oh, oh.

Business of the House

It will not be delayed so long because of me, I am simply guessing that it is not going to pass in a day or two. The government should be able to assess the position.
I see in the house today many hon. members who have children. I am sure most of them have. If we are to have a recess we do not want one in October or November; we should be able to arrange our business so as to have one in July and August. Again the Prime Minister laughs. Maybe he has no children of school age. Maybe he does not want a holiday in July and August. I do not really know what he wants.
We want to get some business done.

I do know that he has not been very fair to the backbenchers of this house, and I do not think he has been fair with the other political parties. I say this because I believe he must have some time table and he must have some preference. I should like him to give us some assurance. He is not only playing with parliament, as things are now; he is playing with all the people who are writing to me and asking "Will my children be able to go to school this fall; are family allowances to be increased, because unless we know we shall not be able to send our children on to school?" The Prime Minister is not being fair to them. He is not being fair to those who are going to college this fall.
It seems to me that the country is concerned with this matter, and the government has a responsibility in this direction. We should be given a much clearer indication of what legislation the government intend to present, and I think they can count on my support as well as on the support of most hon. members in this house, if they are fair and honest with us. Before a motion of this kind is passed I think hon. members opposite should make their intentions clear, otherwise the country is going to take a hard look at the kind of irresponsibility which the Prime Minister represents.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I did not intend to say anything, and would not have risen had someone on the government side responded to the very reasonable request which has been put forward from this side of the house. The request is simply this: What is the meaning of the words "until adjournment for a summer recess"? Surely some date could be set so that people

could make plans. If the phrase has no meaning, I suggest it be struck out.
There is a question of good faith here. The hon. member who spoke before me made a very reasonable plea for those in this house who have families. How in the world are they ever to have a chance to get to know their children unless they are given an opportunity during the summertime? It is a ridiculous situation that this house should sit throughout the summer without making provision for some of these matters. I agree with an extension of hours, but if this is to be a permanent feature, and if the government does not grant a summer recess, it may of course go on perhaps until December, and in those circumstances I would want to suggest a modification of the hours while still granting the same number of hours for the entire week because I am a firm believer in an extension of the hours of sitting of this house. Could we not have from the government a statement with regard to the meaning of "until adjournment for a summer recess"? I ask that question for this other reason. I heard the Prime Minister over the radio two or three days ago talking in very vigorous terms about what this house was going to do, and he said, with regard to some of the questions before us, "We are going to sit here until we are finished".
Oh, he is playing politics again.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I would not suggest that. This is just a question of good faith. We reached an amicable arrangement yesterday in our various meetings and we are not disposed to debate this debatable motion today. We are quite prepared to put it through, but could we not have an answer from the government side; otherwise, if we do not get an answer, I am sure there will be other members who will want to press the point. So let us have the answer now and perhaps we could pass this motion immediately.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will be very glad at the beginning of the week to make a detailed statement on the business which the government would like to see completed before we consider an Easter recess-
Oh, oh.

-a summer recess. I do not think we will go until Easter, but you never know. I also agree with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that if we can fix a target date, that would be a good thing to do.

But if we fix a target date that we are not able to keep, I hope the government will not be blamed for having misled the house; because we can put forward what we consider to be the most important legislation but that does not mean we will get that legislation through in a week, a month, two months or three months. This week we asked for one month's interim supply, because if we had asked for three months we would perhaps be here all summer debating three months' supply. We asked for one month's interim supply, which we have been debating all week. So what is the use of suggesting that we could finish what we have to do on a certain date when we have no idea how long the house will take on matters such as interim supply? We have decided to go ahead with the flag resolution, a matter which the right hon. Leader of the Opposition called a triviality but to which we attach the greatest possible importance.
Hear, hear.

When we dispose of that resolution we will be able to introduce into the house other priority matters, which I will mention next week. But the country is told by hon. gentlemen opposite that they are going to debate the flag resolution all summer if necessary.
Oh, oh.
If that is the situation, how can we fix a target date or any other kind of date?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder
whether the Prime Minister would permit a question.
Of course.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: If he is still uncertain as to the subjects he wants discussed by this house during the course of the summer and cannot make that announcement until Monday, would it not be wise to hold this motion over until Monday so we can find out whether these words "adjournment for a summer recess" are put there in good faith?
Hear, hear.

They are, of course, put there in good faith. If I make a statement now it cannot necessarily be detailed as to the order of priority from day to day and week to week regarding which measures should be brought forward, because obviously these situations change, which makes it necessary to change the business of the house. That is inevitable.
Business of the House
What we have been doing this week shows that.
But there are certain measures-I said this in the house and I do not mind repeating it -that we consider should be dealt with before we consider the question of a summer recess. The flag resolution is one; the extension of children's allowances is another; loans for students is a third; fiscal relations with the provinces is an essential, including new arrangements for contracting out. It is very important to get this through the house and before the provinces for action. The National Defence Act amendment is another. The pension legislation, in so far as we can get that completed, is a very important matter. It may not be possible to do that before a summer recess. But these are priority matters, and there are others.
There is no use my giving a categorical statement that unless we cannot get all these matters through we cannot adjourn for the summer, because we have to make our time table correspond to the realities of parliamentary discussion, and those realities are determined more by hon. gentlemen opposite than by us on this side.
Perhaps I might add this, Mr. Speaker, because I think it is a very practical suggestion. While it is important to extend the hours of sitting at this time, and perhaps we should revise our hours of sitting for the future indefinitely, it is even more important to make arrangements as to the amount of time which should be devoted to any particular piece of legislation. If we can do that then indeed we can set a target date, because if we bring forward four or five pieces of legislation and can agree with hon. gentlemen opposite that we will have three days on one piece of legislation, four days on another, two days on another-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: One day for the flag.
-then we would know where we are going and how long it would take us to get there.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is closure.

We have been putting this suggestion forward for years. The hon. gentleman opposite just said that is closure. If they take that attitude to a constructive arrangement regarding the business to be put before the house which would mean we would know how much time would be taken on each piece of legislation, and call that closure, this explains why in the committee on procedure we cannot get anywhere on this matter.

Business of the House

Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister a question before he sits down. With reference to the legislation he has mentioned, can we have some assurance that by at least the middle of next week all this legislation will be on the order paper, so we will have some opportunity to study it? The Prime Minister has already mentioned items which we have not seen and have had no opportunity to study.

There is a resolution in Votes and Proceedings today regarding youths' allowances. We will get the resolution regarding student loans on the order paper as quickly as possible. The only reason it is being held up is the difficulties with the provinces; because we have to clear these matters with the provinces, particularly this matter. As soon as we can get the agreement of the provinces as to the actual terms of the resolution, it will go on the order paper at once; and that applies to the pension legislation.
Then it is not we who are holding it up.

With reference to the Canada pension plan, if it cannot be dealt with until the fall there is perhaps no immediate hurry in this regard; but if the Prime Minister wants this matter dealt with before a summer recess we should certainly have a white paper and a bill put before us very soon.

I agree that the house should have a white paper before the pension legislation is dealt with, and we will do our best to have that white paper in print and circulated within the next two or three weeks.

I noticed that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) was concerned about the fathers of young families, who sit in the house. I can tell him that I have eight children whose ages range from 19 months to 15 years, but my wife and my children are prepared to give up their holidays so that we may give our country a distinctive flag as soon as possible.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister made a statement with regard to the importance which the government attached to the flag resolution. I do not want to enter into a discussion on that matter; there is a time and a place to debate

that, which is when the resolution is before the house. But I do want to point out that it was with this in mind that on May 25 last I asked the right hon. gentleman this question:
I wonder whether the Prime Minister could indicate whether the resolution on the flag, if there is to be one, when introduced will be one of the items to which he referred on May 15-
That was when he gave the long, detailed list of legislation to which the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre referred. I then gave in my question this particular citation. Then I asked the right hon. gentleman this supplementary question:
Would the Prime Minister indicate whether it is his view that considering the importance the government attaches to this matter, when debate is once entered into it should continue without being interrupted by other government legislation, and that each member wishing to make a contribution should have ample opportunity to do so?
The right hon. gentleman said that he thought that was a very reasonable suggestion. I point this out, that when the government placed the resolution on the order paper, in the light of this answer they could only have anticipated that there would be a lengthy and undoubtedly acrimonious debate. Consequently that must be taken into consideration, having in mind the other items which the government has suggested they want completed before we have a summer recess. Putting this motion on the order paper at that particular time and under the circumstances could have led to nothing else than taking up the time that is apparently going to elapse before any recess will be available.

Mr. Speaker, I heard several members of the opposition ask the Prime Minister to set a date for the summer recess.
A proverb says that the government ordinarily decides when the session will start but the opposition decides when it will end. The opposition, as we know, always has the possibility to discuss any piece of legislation as long as it pleases.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, to organize the business of the house in a satisfactory manner, the Prime Minister should first prepare a list of the most important measures he wants the house to pass; he should discuss them with representatives of the various opposition parties. It is at a round table that those representatives of the house will succeed in setting the date of the summer recess for those who want to spend the summer holidays with

their families. The way things are going at the present time, that is rather difficult. If the Prime Minister gives us a list of measures and the opposition is not ready to accept it in full, further discussion or compromise between the party in office and the opposition parties is impossible.
I wonder why the Prime Minister does not, instead, make up a list which he would then submit to the representatives of each of the opposition parties. Then, the opposition parties could decide-as is normally the case, since it is the responsibility of the opposition to criticize the legislation put forward by the government-about the intersession period. I think that this would be the best procedure and it would be better than having the Prime Minister enumerate the bills he would like to have passed before the summer recess. By submitting such a list, there would be no possible compromise as to deciding on the date of a summer recess.
For instance, I can assure the Prime Minister that our party would be willing to pass resolution No. 44a as quickly as possible, but resolution No. 44b not so quickly. As a matter of fact, it is under such circumstances that a compromise can be arrived at, in order to expedite the business of the house.
That is the suggestion we are making to the Prime Minister and to the government house leader, so that the business of the house may be expedited.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has just stated once again that the flag issue must be settled before we recess for our summer holidays. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that a request has been made to call a plebiscite on this matter, but this request for a plebiscite was denied, the reason being that the Prime Minister was well aware of the outcome and the fate of this flag issue if the plebiscite were taken. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister is using this issue as a club over the opposition's head and trying to make them submit to his decision on the flag.
Order. The matter under discussion is the hours of sitting. I wonder whether we could restrict ourselves to that.

Mr. Speaker, this is the item I am speaking to. The Prime Minister is using this issue as a club over the opposition's head; he is using loss of holidays and no summer recess as a means to force the opposition into submission on the flag issue;, one
Business of the House
which he knows will not carry in this Canada of ours.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has indicated to the house on more than one occasion that he believes members of the house should have every possible opportunity to express their views as to how they feel about a flag design for Canada, whether it is his flag design or someone else's. He has also indicated that he wants a free and full discussion of the matter. I cannot see how he relates his feelings in this regard, in view of the fact that if each hon. member in the house were to indicate his views in a 15 minute speech the debate would extend almost through the summer holiday season, with his statement today that the flag issue must be settled before we have a summer holiday.
While I am sure we all agree that the flag Issue is an important matter, it is one which the Prime Minister promised the Canadian people, he says, within two years of his taking office. The two years do not expire until April 1965. I am sure if he is fair to the members of the House of Commons-and at the same time April 1965 is well within the limits of his solemn pledge-he will agree to set this matter aside, as it is an emotional issue, and consider placing legislation before the house of immediate importance to the Canadian public.
I would ask him not to go forward with this flag debate with the great urgency which he now indicates, placing it before every possible piece of legislation on the order paper, as well as other legislation not yet on the order paper but which is to come. I would ask him to give hon. members the opportunity to be deliberate in their considerations; to give them an opportunity to benefit by the views of other members in the house so they can determine what should be their stand; and I ask him not to set any kind of time limit or to place any impediment on any hon. member with regard to when this matter should be debated and for how long. In view of the fact that we have until April 1965 I would hope that we could take the four immediate necessary steps which will be of benefit to the economy of the country and the Canadian people, rather than forcing this issue to the forefront and setting aside these other matters which were also promised and supposedly so urgent.
Oh, oh.

I do not know why hon. members are interrupting me.

Business of the House
We want you to sit down.

The Prime Minister has not brought forward legislation which he promised the Canadian people over a year ago, and I think he should take steps to do so rather than to force through something which he did not promise the people of Canada until 1965. That is the question in the minds of most people in Canada.
Oh, oh.
Mr. Speaker, I have asked the Prime Minister on many occasions-
Sit down.
-to proceed with other legislation which would be of greater benefit to the Canadian people and the Canadian nation than forcing this flag debate on this house.
Order. I understand the hon. member has just finished.

Mr. Speaker, if there was any understanding in the house as to where we were going this morning it seems to me it has been completely obliterated by the remarks of the Prime Minister. I for one resent very much his suggestion that he keeps throwing out to the effect that the delay in the business of this house is in any way occasioned by the actions of opposition parties.
Let us just consider that suggestion for a moment. It was not too many weeks ago that the Prime Minister got up and gave the house a list of some 38 items which he wanted to have passed before a summer recess. Then suddenly out of the blue came the flag, about which we heard nothing. The Prime Minister objects to the official opposition registering their views on the flag, and his backbenchers call it a filibuster. I do not agree with the official opposition on the flag issue, but they hold their views seriously and they insist upon stating them. I say that when the Prime Minister brought in the flag resolution he knew he was sabotaging his own legislative program.
We all know the views that many members of the official opposition hold, and we know they intend to express them. The government knew that; the Prime Minister knew that. Yet he precipitated the issue of the flag; and when he persists in having it deal with before a summer recess he knows there is not going to be a recess and we might as well stop talking about it. I know that as far
[Mr. Coates.l
as I am concerned, and the other members of our party, I believe, I am sure we can forget all about a recess because if he is going to insist on the flag issue being dealt with in addition to these legislative items, if he is really sincere about dealing with them, there is not going to be a summer recess at all.
We want to deal with these matters, and we are prepared to sit here and deal with them. But it does not lie in the Prime Minister's mouth to come here and say that the fault lies with the official opposition, and then say that he cannot even bring in the family allowance legislation because he has not reached agreement with the provinces. This is his responsibility, and the fault lies on his head. Then he tells us this morning that we have to deal with financial arrangements with the provinces, something we had not heard about.
It is on the order paper now.

It has suddenly appeared out of nowhere. We have been asking that the student loan legislation be brought before us. All I am trying to point out, and I think it should be made clear, is that this is certainly the most stupidly and illogically organized legislative program within our memory, and that the fault for this lies squarely on the heads of the government. There is really no point in passing this motion now because we are going to be here all summer, and we may as well make up our minds to that at this time.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support some of the comments of the previous speaker and to make a few of my own with regard to the motion. We in the official opposition agreed to the presentation of the motion. We will support it, and I hope it will pass before one o'clock. We have agreed to it simply because we feel there are legislative items that must come forward. This has been said before. But what bothers me is that there are quite a number of items on the order paper which have to be referred to committees if a reasonable amount of work is going to be done on them in committee. Surely these matters could be brought forward immediately and referred to committees.
We have talked about different items. The hon. member for Timiskaming mentioned three. I agree with him that they require immediate consideration, particularly the student loan legislation. Yesterday we tried to obtain a commitment to have that item

brought forward, and today the Prime Minister has made an explanation involving the provinces. I brought up this matter yesterday on a non-political basis, and it was the Liberal members who laughed at my suggestion and tried to howl me down. I was extremely serious about the matter because I am closely associated with the problem. We want this legislation brought forward immediately.
With regard to the flag debate, I should like to say that following the invitation extended to us by the Prime Minister I have asked, not demanded, that anyone who has strong views in this regard should express them in the house on the basis of that invitation. We are now prepared to go forward on that basis. We have one amendment before us now. How many more amendments will there be? No one in the house knows, but there is no question but that if other legislative items are not brought forward before the flag debate continues there will be no summer recess.
This does not particularly concern me. I am one who believes I must express my views in regard to the flag question whether I want to or not because the people of my constituency have strong feelings on this matter. They are now asking what is the matter with parliament. I say, Mr. Speaker, that if we do not have some decent organization of our business the people of the country will have good reason to lose faith in this parliament.
Not only has the government made one horrible mess of the presentation of legislation but the situation in the house is, I must admit, equally as bad. That has been shown this morning, Mr. Speaker. But you cannot expect a responsible attitude on the part of members in the house if we do not have a responsible presentation of what the country really needs. There can be a lot done for the country if the Prime Minister will bring forward legislation that is good for the country. I know that is the opinion of the people of the country. He can certainly set back the flag debate and bring this legislation forward. This is what the people of Canada want.
We promised yesterday that we would cooperate in regard to student loans, something that we feel is very necessary, and the Prime Minister will receive equal co-operation on every other basically good piece of legislation he brings forward. But we do not want to be muzzled on the flag debate. Members can make their speeches on that subject at any time. When I have made my speech somebody else can rise and make his speech. I plead with the Prime Minister in the name of common sense not to mislead us where
Business of the House
Canada's affairs and the flag question are concerned. We intend to support the motion.

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question. He indicated in his very interesting remarks that there are certain things on the order paper that should go to committee where they could be given immediate consideration. Is he speaking on behalf of his party on this matter, and if we bring these matters forward at once will he give us his assurance that they will be referred to committee without any delay?
Oh, oh.
Without debate?
More muzzling.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will say for the party I have the honour to represent that if the Prime Minister will present these matters to the house, we will see that they are properly dealt with.

Mr. Speaker, I have to support in essence what the hon. member for Danforth said a few moments ago. In addition, however, one or two very legitimate requests have been made to the Prime Minister which have not been answered properly yet. For example, in the resolution before us there is specific reference to a summer recess. During the course of the debate more than one member has asked the Prime Minister to give some indication of what the target date is for the summer recess. In my opinion he has given an unsatisfactory answer by saying there are X number of things that must be done, and that the government has no control over how long they will take.
I should like to remind the Prime Minister that last fall there was an enormous amount of work piled up, what might almost be called a backlog, before December 20, the target date for prorogation. If he will turn his mind back to those days he will recall that there was an enormous amount of work in the form of estimates and legislation which went through very quickly during the final week.
There are times when debates on legislation and estimates seem not to be making much progress and appear to be bogged down, but if we did have a target date for a summer recess some of these matters could probably be expedited very rapidly just before reaching that date. I think it is a little unreasonable on the part of the Prime Minister

Business of the House
and the government that they will not give any indication of what date they have in mind for the summer recess, when in fact there is reference to summer recess in the motion they are asking us to pass.
I think these matters can be worked out. The flag debate is one that perhaps will not be concluded expeditiously. But if the Prime Minister would undertake to give us a list of those things that have to go through before a summer recess, and some kind of target date, I do not believe the members of the opposition would hold him to the order he set out, that there must be the flag debate first, then family allowances, student loans and so on. This is the prerogative of the government, to change the order as time progresses. The Prime Minister indicated today that things change; therefore the government has to have the right to change the order.
I believe we should consider some of the suggestions that have been made from this side of the house, and there would be cooperation to expedite many of the things the government wants to get through. If they would give us some indication of a target date probably they would get still more cooperation.

Mr. Speaker, once again this year we are witnessing an attempt at blackmail about a summer recess. The Prime Minister and the government have decided to use that trick to force the hand of other opposition parties.
As far as I am concerned, I support a distinctive national flag. But I should have liked the government to use a normal procedure so that the members of the house could put their views forward on that matter. The present action followed by the government means that every day we have a little more blackmail. Every day, they try to exercise coercion through the promise of a summer recess as if we were school kids being told: "If you are good children you shall get a holiday."
I think that such a policy is lacking in elegance. I also think that the government has absolutely no sense of organization as regards the business of the house.
Reference is made to family allowances, which are excessively important, and on which legislation should be passed before the summer recess. We are told that the student loans legislation should be passed before the summer recess. Besides, as a representative from a rural riding, I think that

that there is one thing we must do before the summer recess, and that is to pass an appropriate legislation to give assistance to Quebec farmers in order to remedy the high cost of feed grain.
I feel the government should take its responsibilities, stop its childish blackmail about the summer recess and deal with the economic problems of the country. Let it say simply and frankly that there will be no summer recess. However, if the Prime Minister is sincere and absolutely wants a summer recess, let him meet with the other party leaders in order to straighten out a situation which is becoming awful and which is turning this parliament into a laughingstock in the eyes of Canadians. If the government wants us to pass its legislation, let it set out a final program.
Yesterday, the Prime Minister mentioned two or three pieces of legislation which he wants to see passed before the summer recess. This morning again he added another one, of the utmost importance, concerning fiscal relations with the provinces. The house has never been able to pass such a matter in a few hours. I am convinced that when the Prime Minister arrives in the house next Monday, he will add two or three new measures to those he has already suggested and, if he speaks on Tuesday, he will add some more.
It is getting to be a joke which has lasted long enough. The Prime Minister should sit, think over the situation and stop his childish blackmail tricks.
So far as the remarks of the hon. member for Medicine Hat are concerned, I have already-
Order. How does the Prime Minister get the floor?
I have been asked a question.
What about a second speech? Are we all to have second speeches? Surely this question could have been answered by the mover of the resolution.

Then may I ask the hon. gentleman who has just sat down a question. Would he agree that it would be desirable on Monday for the house leaders to get together and discuss the various suggestions that have been made in this debate this morning, the desirability of setting a target date, when that target date should be, a list of the legislation and other proposals which should be disposed of before the summer vacation? Will

my hon. friend who has made these remarks agree that there should be a meeting of this kind where we can work out the program in detail, and will he give me the assurance that the house leader for his party will attend such a meeting?

That is a case of the old
excuse, the old alibi.
May I ask the Prime Minister a question. Would it be acceptable if the leaders of the parties discussed this matter, because we feel it is an important matter that should be considered at that level.

That is a very useful suggestion; perhaps a meeting should take place between the leaders of the parties rather than the house leaders, because we have had great difficulty in getting full representation at the house leaders' meetings in the last two months.

The rules are the rules, and the Prime Minister had no business getting up and making a gratuitous statement like that. The responsibility for the difficulties of parliament rests on his shoulders and his inability to organize.

I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. The right hon. gentleman is quite right. The responsibility rests on my shoulders: that is why I am so discouraged when we have these meetings of house leaders. His house leader has not attended, and indicated yesterday he would not attend.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I rise on a question of privilege to deal with this statement by the Prime Minister, who has crawled into the gutter again, as he said with regard to me just a few days ago.

I wonder, in view of the fact that there are only ten minutes remaining, if we could not reach some conclusion this morning. The atmosphere seems to be heating up continuously. We have a motion to discuss, and surely we could dispose of it by one o'clock.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I appreciate your desire, Mr. Speaker. Half an hour ago I suggested that there would be no debate on this issue if someone on the government side would tell us whether this phrase in the resolution was put there in good faith or just as a trap. Now we know that this was put in as a trap to conceal their intention.
The Prime Minister has gratutiously made an attack on me with regard to my objection
Business of the House
to attend the meetings of house leaders. I desisted attending those meetings of house leaders, and for very good reasons; one, they were not confidential; two, there was a combination of people trying to put me and the party I represent in a false position-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
-three, a member of that house committee divulged items that had passed at those meetings and did not tell the true facts. I said never again would I attend a meeting of house leaders in the presence of that hon. member, and I have not. The Prime Minister has no right to inject these accusations into the debate this morning. It shows the level on which he operates, trying to gain some partisan political advantage out of the statement in the house.
Now he has caused the deterioration of this debate and its prolongation because of his complete incompetence in managing the business of the House of Commons. All he had to do, in response to a reasonable request by the Leader of the Opposition and by the leader of the New Democratic party, was to say he would postpone this motion as I suggested and we would see if we could not come to an agreement over the lunch hour. Let us support this, I suggested, and we will see if we cannot come to an agreement over the lunch hour. That is exactly what could have been done, but oh no, he has held the club over us. He has told us he is going to drive things through despite anything we may wish to do, and is attempting to trap us with an extension of hours so he can get on with something he has produced in the way of a flag and is insisting that this house pass. It is the act of a man who is becoming drunk with power and is showing signs of dictatorship. I ask him to withdraw the remarks he made with regard to me concerning meetings of house leaders.

Mr. Speaker, as one drunk with power I am a little worried about getting on my feet, but may I tell the hon. gentleman who just sat down that I stated a fact, that he did not attend house leaders' meetings for a long time, and he has admitted that himself. I made no allegation or accusation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: An insinuation.

It was explaining why I did not attend. May I ask the Leader of the Opposition this question. If we can arrange this kind of meeting I have been talking

Business of the House
about, with the house leaders, to work out a program by agreement-
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, how does the Prime Minister get the floor? This is his third speech. The mover of the resolution can do this, but not the Prime Minister.

It seems to me we are at long last approaching some conclusion on this matter of time and subjects and hours, and surely we can reach some sort of agreement by one o'clock. Therefore in that context surely the Prime Minister has almost a duty to suggest to hon. members of the house anything which will assist the house in reaching a conclusion which will be of assistance to the house itself.

Mr. Speaker, the mover of the motion has the right, but surely Your Honour is not making a statement to the effect that any time the Prime Minister wants to get up he can do so, having once spoken. It is for the mover of the resolution to do this.
Mr. Speaker, the very short question I was about to ask, with the permission of the house-

On a point of privilege, Mr. Speaker-and I am very sorry to have to get up on a point of privilege when the right hon. Prime Minister is on his feet-I think it is time we made very clear for the benefit of hon. members like myself whether the house is meeting with the Speaker in the chair or whether we are meeting in committee of the whole. It is quite obvious that the procedure which has been going on for the past hour has been a procedure in committee of the whole, and I know there are a few hon. members like myself who want to have something to say when the Speaker is in the chair. Therefore, sir, with all deference to yourself, and although it is now five minutes to one o'clock, I want the right to speak with the Speaker in the chair and not with the house in committee of the whole, to enable me to make my point of view known.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

All I want to say is that since we have been in the whole so long, can we not adjourn for lunch and come back with the Speaker in the chair, and hope at an agreed time to bring this matter to a satisfactory conclusion?
I would just like to say that if the Minister of Justice speaks now he will close the debate.

In view of what I have just said I could not possibly agree to that. I think, Mr. Speaker, I am not being at all unfair in asking the opportunity to speak on this matter. This session I have not risen to speak very often in the House of Commons, one reason being that due to the way the session has been carried on I have found that more effective work can be done in committees.
We have before us now a most interesting and far reaching resolution. At the time it was moved this morning by the Minister of Justice as house leader I was prepared to accept and support it, but because of the statement made by the Prime Minister I am not certain at the moment as to whether it can or should be supported at this time, or whether it should be postponed for reconsideration after what I hope will be a meeting, between now and Monday, of the leaders of all parties represented in the house to go into a full discussion as to government business.
What has brought me to change my mind, in a period of approximately one hour, on a statement made by the Prime Minister? It is this, sir; that the Prime Minister, whether he leads a minority or majority government, has the responsibility and the authority, and I would hope the prestige, of leading this House of Commons. This morning has given us complete proof that the Prime Minister is not prepared to accept that prestige and responsibility.
I am going to ask the Prime Minister if he will not have the intestinal fortitude and courage to admit a mistake and make a withdrawal. Ninety per cent of our problem today, and for the past days and weeks, arises because of his personal view, opinion, pride and prestige on the flag issue. If the Prime Minister would accept the fact that a decision on the flag issue could be postponed until in November or December, we would be a lot closer to agreement; because, sir, the flag issue, emotional, sentimental and important as it is, is not a question on which a decision before a summer recess will fill one belly of one person in Canada.
May I call it one o'clock Mr. Speaker.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.

At the time of the adjournment at one o'clock

I had the privilege of addressing this honourable house for approximately five minutes. In that period of time, short as it was, I endeavoured to make clear my views as a parliamentarian and I put forward certain expressions of opinion to the Prime Minister.
Now that I have a few minutes left this afternoon, I should like in part to repeat what I said and then to follow through with certain recommendations. Although the Prime Minister is not here, I should like to say to him through you, Mr. Speaker, that I understand, or at least I hope I do, the responsibility which rests with that high office.
He is here now.

Of course, I have never had the honour of occupying the position of Prime Minister or premier of a province, but for 12 years I did have the honour of being the leader of the loyal opposition in a province, so I think I know something about the meaning of the word "responsibility". In particular, I am familiar with situations where someone in high office thinks he has made a mistake. What I was trying to express, through you, sir, to the Prime Minister, was this: Never be afraid to admit a mistake or an error in tactics or strategy. If my experience over 31 years means anything it is that people honour a man who will admit a mistake, whether in policy, tactics or strategy. I am being a little impudent in what I am about to say now, but it is my personal belief that our Prime Minister today is not the man this country requires because of a strange mix-up in his personality.
Shame.

I think I get the import of some of the hon. members remarks, but the question before the house concerns the hours of sitting, and an analysis of the personality of some other member of the house, even if he is a high official, does not in my view come within the general orbit.

That is the basis of my introduction to this particular matter; it explains why we have a motion such as this before us, now. I am not in the least being disrespectful. As a matter of fact I am being one of the honest persons speaking on this measure. I am simply saying that this is one of the reasons we are faced with this problem- the personality of a prime minister who ties together being a professor, a civil servant, a secretary of state for external affairs and leader of a government.
Business of the House
Order.

Understanding that, is the basis for understanding the problem we are facing right now in the motion before us. You will surely not call me to order, Mr. Speaker, if I express this view and express the hope, as I did indirectly before one o'clock, that the Prime Minister will recognize this fact and exercise more authority and leadership in the conduct of this house and the presentation of government business. I am actually trying not only to be honest and sincere but to explain why I wish to bring in certain recommendations. Only on the basis of understanding the personality of the Prime Minister can I bring in what I wish to recommend. I am asking the Prime Minister if he will recognize the position in which we find ourselves-and I use the word "we" for the majority of members of this house who wish to get on with the people's business. The majority of members, having missed an Easter recess-if they did as I did, and stayed here-want a summer recess. But the Prime Minister has laid it down that there will not be a summer recess unless certain things are done and certain priorities dealt with. And the one factor which will hold up the recess is the flag issue.
Hear, hear.

I ask the Prime Minister again if he will not recognize that making this issue a priority matter to be decided while sitting additional hours, before a recess can be considered, proceeds from personal pride-it has to be done because he thinks he would otherwise lose something in the eyes of members of this house and the people of Canada.
When we discuss additional hours we also discuss the statement of the Prime Minister this morning as to the business. I am asking that the Prime Minister have the intestinal fortitude to state that public business comes before personal pride and decision and that the matter of the flag shall not be a deciding factor.
Mr. Speaker, I have to introduce it that way in order to come to my next point, namely that the Prime Minister cannot make that decision which I and, I think, other members request him to make, unless the official opposition will accept a sense of responsibility, decency, dignity and decorum in the House of Commons. Day after day and week after week during this session we have seen, not the getting on with the public business from the official opposition but the utilizing of par-

Business of the House
liament as a sounding board, hoping to get an election, in making campaign speeches in this house.
What are you doing now?
I have run 11 times and I have been elected 11 times-and not one of you can make that statement.
Are you boasting, or complaining?
My position is this. I ask the Prime Minister to give consideration-
This is humility at its greatest.

-to this proposal, that before a summer recess we shall deal with the business that affects the health, welfare, wealth and security of the people of Canada and postpone until after a recess, in the fall, a decision on the flag. I say we have not the right and I have not the right to ask the Prime Minister to consider this unless the leader of the official opposition and the Tories behind him will agree to it and will also agree not to throw out the continual challenge of "Retreat" and "Resign". In other words, Mr. Speaker, if the official opposition will accept responsibility along this line that I am proposing to the Prime Minister, I think there might be a basis of agreement, understanding, and a recess, I would hope, not later than the middle of August.
Oh, oh.

I say not later than the middle of August because if we are going to deal with student loans, family allowances, the Canada pension plan and those things that we should do before we leave here, this cannot be before the middle of August if it is done on a proper and efficient basis; whereas if the flag is to maintain its priority, if the official opposition are going to carry on, when that resolution is again before us, as they have in the past, there will be no recess whatsoever. So, Mr. Speaker, having given considerable thought to this question over the lunch hour I should like to try to consolidate my views in this way, which I offer for the consideration of Your Honour, the government and all members. I would like to ask for the consideration of the Prime Minister, the government, the leader of the official opposition and their supporters of the following five points:
1. That the present motion which we are now discussing stand, with the exception of

a special amendment to grant employees in the House of Commons a holiday on July 1.
2.	That the Prime Minister call a meeting of all party leaders and discuss government business, with the objective of reaching a unanimous or majority opinion.
3.	That if the decision is not unanimous, with only one party abstaining from the agreement, the House of Commons be informed as to that party and their basis of disagreement.
This is a new manifesto.

I just heard someone say this was a new manifesto, and by heavens I think it is a good one for the House of Commons to consider.
4.	That the Prime Minister agree to drop the priority of the flag decision until the fall, and that if this is agreed to, the official opposition shall be asked not to practise political expediency by terming it a retreat or a call for a general election.
5.	That every measure be taken to expedite the recommendations from the committee on house procedure relative to hours and method of conducting the House of Commons business and, if the same is stymied or stalemated in any way by any party representative at meetings, or refusal to attend, this should be immediately reported to the House of Commons and the House of Commons should be given the opportunity of voting upon, and thereby deciding, any majority report dealing with recommendations to expedite the business of the House of Commons whilst at the same time retaining a most reasonable opportunity for members to express their opinions as the elected representatives of their constituents.
Amen.
My hon. friend says amen. I was waiting for somebody on my right to say hallelujah.
Hallelujah.

I say, Mr. Speaker, it will be amen and hallelujah if we in this House of Commons now, after the sittings we have held this session, can get down to carrying out the business of the people in a calm, efficient and proper manner. So. Mr. Speaker, I am now going to conclude-
Hear, hear.

I notice sir, that when I said I was going to conclude the applause came from those on my left, who apparently do
not realize the importance of the matters

which I am trying to draw to the attention of this house. I conclude, Mr. Speaker, after having made a special appeal, through you, to the Prime Minister, to the leader of the official opposition and to all hon. members to get on with the business of the people. I think we can do this and can reach conclusions on these matters. There may be a possibility of a recess at the latter part of August if we will remember those most famous words-and I love them and am going to give them to the House of Commons-of Henry Ward Beecher-
Who?
Mr. Speaker, I am being interrupted by some imbecilic remark from the left.
Shame.

May I ask all members of parliament to remember these words, in view of our discussion this morning and this afternoon on our procedures and what could forestall a recess. Henry Ward Beecher said this:
A thoughtful mind sees not the flag alone but the nation itself-the principles, the truths, the history.
We should remind ourselves through you, Mr. Speaker, that if we can submerge pride, prejudice and political expediency and remember those words, then I say we will have been, and will be, worthy representatives of those who elected us and sent us to the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I see that the house leader is very anxious to close the debate, but I am not sure he will be able to answer some of the criticisms or the logic of the perfectly understandable complaints which have been made about the handling of business by the government. Certainly when we are considering whether we should sit longer hours some of the questions we should ask ourselves are: Is this the best and only way we can run the business? What is necessary that should be done? What is the urgent business? How can we streamline the way in which we work? I submit that all these are legitimate factors to consider when discussing this resolution.
I was much impressed with the calmness and logical approach of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates). He has been rather vehement in his feelings on the flag issue, but I thought he gave an example to hon. members of calm and logical discussion. The speech of the hon. member for Danforth
Business of the House
(Mr. Scott) was, I thought, a model of logic very forcefully presented. If the government will look at what the speech contains they will find some very unanswerable reasons why the government should proceed with the legislation most necessary to the economic well being of the nation rather than that piece of legislation which is a sop to the vanity of the government, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and some of the members on that side.
I think most of us in this house regret that co-operation among house leaders has broken down; but I for one in this party will state frankly that I have advised my house leader that I could not condone his taking part in any consultation so long as those consultations were not confidential as they were in the past. Since the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) made it so plain that he refuses to recognize this confidentiality it is impossible to carry on worth-while discussions, and so long as he represents the New Democratic party I advised our house leader that he should not conduct what would only be farcical negotiations.
I remember the events just before Easter very well. I remember what the Prime Minister said had to be completed. He knew interim supply had to be passed and he wanted the supplementary estimates passed. We had made requests that essential matters be brought in and he continued to dilly-dally. At last the suggestion was made: "If you want an Easter holiday, pass this now". In other words, they waste the time of the house with non-essentials, bring forward the essentials just before a holiday, and say to the members of the house that the only way we can get a holiday is by abandoning business worth discussing and passing it without comment. I had thought that if there was one thing the government should have learned it was that in this house they cannot get away with using a club. Members of the house are a little weary. We would all like a summer recess. But I doubt, Mr. Speaker, you would find very many who are willing to abandon their duty to examine government measures and legislation closely and will knuckle under to this sort of blackmail by the Prime Minister. I think the tactics are deplorable.
I hope the press will analyse exactly what the Prime Minister has been doing.
Hear, hear.

I am glad that that remark has been met with enthusiasm. Perhaps the press friendly to the Liberal party will now know

Business of the House
in advance that they will be forgiven if they are honest with the party for a change and paint it in its true colours. The Prime Minister has put himself in a position where, in response to questions in the house, he said he hoped that every hon. member interested in the flag would have a chance to speak. I am certain there is not one member in the house who cannot understand the duty of each hon. member on an issue like this. Each of us has to get up and express the view of the area he represents. Therefore it goes without saying that there will be a great many speeches on the flag.
Adoptee.

We are almost 100 years from confederation and suddenly the Prime Minister brings in his pennant. This has to be passed and given top priority after nearly 100 years of confederation. This defies logic. I wonder whether we can look behind the government tactics-

Mr. Speaker, under the rules of the house, any motion similar to the one under consideration is debatable.
However, the rules state that members who take part in the debate must talk to the principle of the motion and not about various subjects unrelated to it.
I am convinced that at the present time groups of fanatics and extremists in this house take advantage of the debate on the motion under consideration to try to forestall the flag resolution forever. I maintain that this is not in accordance with the motion under study but that fanatics are taking advantage of it-
This is no point of order.
One at a time, please. The hon. member for Lapointe.
On a point of privilege, this is no point of order.
The Chair will decide whether it is in order, but I propose to listen to it first.

Mr. Speaker, my point of order is consistent with the provisions of standing order 32, which lists the motions which are debatable. Besides, the same order states that those who take part in a debate of this kind must deal exclusively with the motion. What happens at the present time is

that fanatics and the extremists take advantage of the debate on this motion to kill the resolution we were discussing earlier, namely the resolution concerning the adoption of a flag, and, in my opinion, this is against the rules.

Order, please. The debate ranged this morning quite far and wide, and consequently, although the hon. member was beginning to range far and wide, nevertheless in my opinion he was still in order. I hope hon. members will remember that we are discussing the motion before the house, and should if possible restrict their remarks to the question of the hours of sitting of the house.

Mr. Speaker, we are considering the time of sitting and the extension of hours, and one of the moot questions is whether it is better to extend hours or to do the business of the house some other way. Is it a better way of doing things than passing this resolution; and I submit I did stick to that point. After that intervention by the hon. member for Lapointe the house can see the point I was making about the flag and its urgency now. After 100 years of confederation why does it have to be passed all of a sudden before a summer recess while at the same time so many important matters must of necessity be delayed? I suggest that the only reason the flag issue is regarded by the government with that much urgency is that there is that much pressure on the government from what I will call the lunatic fringe of politics in Canada today-
Oh, oh.

-whose viewpoint is expressed so very well by the hon. member for Lapointe. I think it is clear that the order of business in the house is being arranged to make a good show, to make political propaganda and not to take care of business of the house that is important to the nation. I cannot understand how the government can pretend that they are anxious to bring in pension legislation and not give it priority over the flag debate. I cannot understand how they have the effrontery to say to the people of Canada that they are trying to do the business of the country and yet do it in this manner.
I submit that the Prime Minister has neglected to look very closely at this matter. If he will look at his answers to questions in the house with regard to the flag debate and the urgency of other matters, if he will

reflect for one moment on the amount of time that must of necessity be taken by speeches on the flag, if he will reflect on how important the flag issue is, and that it is necessary for the country to have lots of time to consider the matter so that unanimity may perhaps be achieved throughout the nation in fact before the issue is disposed of, he will realize why it should not take precedence over other legislation.
I am perfectly willing to go along with longer hours of sitting, I am perfectly willing to sit all summer if we must, but I submit that no member of the house is going to be happy sitting longer hours all summer if the government refuses to bring the business of the country before the house in a sensible manner.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say at the outset that the few remarks I am about to make are not intended to waste the time of the house, even though that seems to have become rather current practice recently. Nevertheless, with all due respect to the Chair, I should like to express as objectively as possible the views of a newcomer, of a backbencher, on the motion under consideration.
Members on both sides of the house often say that backbenchers are not always free to speak as they please in various circumstances. That is what I should like to do this afternoon as briefly as possible and without any partisanship.
We are now facing a problem and I regret, like everybody else, that we are not expediting the business of the house as we would like to. We are trying to find adequate means of presenting, at last, to the Canadian people the sound legislation to which they are entitled. I strongly support that policy.
However, we are told that backbenchers should, according to what has been the practice for a relatively long time, rather sit tight and listen to veterans in the house in order to learn a few things about procedure and that they should rely on the veterans' parliamentary experience. I was quite willing to do just that until today. I tried to learn as much as I could but I would like to forget as quickly as possible what I have unfortunately learned in the past few days.
When this so-called experience of the veterans of this house boils down to knowing how to meander around artfully and craftily in parliamentary procedure and politics which 20220-303
Business of the House
go back to the middle ages, I say it is high time we should find a cure.
Is it conceivable, Mr. Speaker, that, right in the middle of this twentieth century, where we have even gone beyond the atomic age, we should still have to rely on a parliamentary system which almost dates back to the time of the caveman? That is something which a backbencher finds hard to understand.
In my opinion, those self-styled veterans of the art of politics, who too often speak with their eyes turned towards the press gallery, so they can see their names in the newspapers the next day or in order to prove how expert they are in parliamentary procedure or else pursue their morbid ambitions, those people should refrain a bit from speaking often.
I think that the only practical advice we can give at this time, Mr. Speaker, is that, while we support the measure which is now before us, although, in my opinion, it does not go far enough, we recommend by common consent to the special parliamentary committee set up to that effect to get to work without delay.
The members of that committee should work 24 hours a day not to amend drastically but to redraft completely the archaic rules of the House of Commons, which often prevent us from going ahead.
With today's political experts, we have to use all kinds of manoeuvres and tactics and we are obliged, in this 20th century, to govern ourselves, to call on citations from Bouri-not and Beauchesne, to go back to 1816, 1600, 1500 or even before Christ.
Mr. Speaker, to begin with, we should insist so as to give ourselves a legislation allowing the backbenchers as well as the front benchers and all the members without exception, the right to speak freely, with much clearer and fewer old-fashioned rules. Then we could go forward and submit legislation, discussing and approving it in the best interests of the Canadian people.
In conclusion I will say, Mr. Speaker, that if we, the backbenchers do not have the political maturity which seems to be so greatly appreciated at times, and rightly so, among the old timers on the political scene who sit in this chamber, we, the backbenchers of the House of Commons can offer, if not trickery and astuteness, at least honesty, frankness, sincerity and the will to work.
That is why, as far as I am concerned, I have already given up the holidays I was anticipating and I am prepared to keep on

Business of the House
working steadily, provided we stop these empty discussions and take the necessary steps so that the house can abandon obsolete rules and start passing legislation in a more modern way.
That will be published in Le Soleil.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when, some time ago, I mean this morning, on orders of the day, I introduced the motion now under discussion, I did so with some satisfaction. Indeed, we have often discussed some of the difficulties which may have existed, when house leaders have to meet, sometimes twice instead of once, and hold double meetings; but finally, we have succeeded, with the co-operation, I must admit, of all house leaders, whom I thought were speaking on behalf of their party, to reach an agreement on this motion. What I mean, and I think it is important that the house should know it, is that during our discussion, no mention was ever made-and I knpw all house leaders will bear me out-of reservations to the passing of this motion by the house.
The only discussions held dealt with the extended hours of sitting, and not with the conditions to impose on the motion.
We suggested at first, and I admit it might not have been the best procedure, that the house should sit on Friday evening, from 8 p.m. to 10 p.m.
The opposition suggested that it would be much better, instead of sitting in the evening, to extend our discussions during the lunch hour. I immediately complied with this request.
Another discussion was held to know whether the house would sit on July 1. We have agreed that the house would celebrate Canada day and that we would not sit on July 1.
I am therefore the first to be surprised at the discussion which took place today.
I hope that each party, trusting his house leader and confirming his word given in good faith, will now pass this motion.
I wish to add this, for the satisfaction of hon. members and to reassure those who were reluctant and who voiced their doubts about the progress of our work. I want to tell the house that on Monday, the right hon. Prime Minister asked me to convene a gathering, or a meeting, of all the house leaders, during which I was to communicate to them the

final priority list with regard to bills or other measures which the government intends to introduce before the end of July. We are to suggest an order of distribution of the hours and days of sittings to allow discussion on all and each of those items, according to their respective importance and the time which each discussion should take.
When we speak of "allocation of time", i.e. the distribution of hours and days of sittings in the house, in order more particularly to discuss one piece of legislation, I think that we should make it clear that this is quite the opposite of the rule of closure.
The allocation or distribution of time to discuss some legislation is agreed upon by all parties in the house; it is opposite of closure, Mr. Speaker.
In this way, each party, considering the kind of legislation or measure to be discussed, would be able to choose among its members those who are particular conversant with the kind of legislation which is to be discussed at a given time or on a given day.
I therefore want to make it clear that this action is essentially connected with full and complete freedom for each party, which is quite the opposite to closure.
I also want to say to hon. members that the right hon. Prime Minister-if the first meeting unfortunately should fail to give definite result-proposes to convene the leaders of all parties in the house to start the procedure all over again and try to come to some conclusion which would help end or close the discussion of priority legislation before the end of July.
I could hardly, when asking the right hon. speechtext:

Particularly, we have been informed 20226-303J
Inquiries of the Ministry that allegations made against Mr. Paul Hall have been denied by him.
But, Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that this is a serious matter, perhaps even more serious in some of the implications that could arise out of it. The officers of the Department of Labour have been on the west coast trying to adjust this situation in a manner which would be equitable and the board of trustees have also-they have jurisdiction over this matter-been on the west coast. Only a few minutes ago I received a telegram, at least it was to the Department of Labour, concerning the negotiations that are taking place, and they are still going on, from the representative of the board of trustees. This telegram reads as follows:
I have met with the parties to the dispute and feel hopeful that a settlement will be reached. The parties are presently considering a proposal of settlement.
I hope that this settlement will be reached today or tomorrow. At the moment, I cannot add anything to what I have already said.

I should like to ask one
supplementary question. The Prime Minister said some of the implications of what I have stated differed from the information he has secured. I secured this information from the same source as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam did.
Will the Prime Minister answer this one question? Did Hall in any way, by the direction that he gave and the arrangements made as to personnel on this ship while it was still in Florida, endeavour to avoid the jurisdiction of the maritime trustees and push in the
S.I.U. as the negotiating body, contrary to what had been the case throughout the years with regard to the three particular classifications I have mentioned?

Mr. Speaker, that has not been so stated in the information I have received but I will take up that specific question with the representatives of the maritime unions, the board of trustees, who are now in Vancouver, and endeavour to obtain a specific answer to that specific question.

The information I have is that the vessel in question, which was formerly operated in southeast United States waters and belongs to the Alaska Trainship Corporation, and which it is hoped by the owners will operate between New Westminster and Alaska, was manned by the
S.I.U. for unlicensed personnel and by the marine engineers beneficial association, for marine engineers, a union which does not operate in Canada and has no Canadian membership.

It is said that the teamsters union, which represents employees of the company which performs the operation of putting railway cars on board the ship, does not question the jurisdiction of the longshoremen's union over this work, but it is also said that the employer concerned objects to the work being done by the I.L.W.U.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask the Minister of Industry a question of which I gave him notice. speechtext:
Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition asked questions along similar lines. I am informed that the government of Quebec is engaged in

Inquiries of the Ministry an endeavour to establish in that province a facility to manufacture motor cars of a type not now made in Canada. This calls for extensive and delicate negotiations with the firms which have designed the cars in question- negotiations to which the government of Canada is not, and has not, been a party.
I would invoke the co-operation of members of the house in not seeking detailed information regarding these negotiations, in the interest of not prejudicing the chance of Canada's acquiring a new manufacturing industry.
In response to the specific queries raised, may I say that the government of Canada has communicated in general terms with the minister of industry and commerce of the province of Quebec concerning the possible manufacture in Canada of European-type cars. Representatives of the government of Quebec yesterday had exploratory discussions with officials of the departments of finance and industry looking to the setting up in Canada of facilities for manufacturing cars of French design.
The Leader of the Opposition also asked: "Is it a fact that officials of the firms in Quebec have been meeting with federal officials within recent weeks?" I would point out that the government of Quebec intends and hopes that the firm which will be manufacturing cars in Canada will be a Canadian controlled firm and will not be a subsidiary of foreign motorcar manufacturers. As a consequence, the negotiations with the federal government will be carried out by or on behalf of the government of Quebec, and not with us, by the foreign motorcar manufacturers.

subtopic: TARIFF CONCESSIONS TO FOREIGN AUTOMOBILE MANUFACTURERS

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: TARIFF CONCESSIONS TO FOREIGN AUTOMOBILE MANUFACTURERS

Up until yesterday there had been no negotiations between officials of the federal government and representatives of these firms.
