The Leader of the Opposition also asked whether the ambassador of France had been in consultation with officials of the Department of Industry or the Department of Finance on this matter. The reply to that question is that the ambassador of France did pay a visit to the Department of Finance to make some inquiries regarding tariff rules and regulations which might be applicable to the import of cars into this country. It was not the purpose of the ambassador, I am informed, to negotiate on this particular occasion, but merely to seek information.
The Leader of the Opposition also asked what was the policy of the government in relation to this transaction. I think the policy of the government has been fairly clearly enunciated. It is to foster the healthy economic growth of manufacturing industry in Canada. To this end the federal government is prepared to do, and will do, all it appropriately can to bring to Canada these additional manufacturing facilities.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a few weeks ago I asked the Prime Minister whether he would consider a study being made of the economic, social and political effects on the rest of Canada of separation, in view of the need for clarification of this subject. At that time he indicated that he would have hoped to give consideration to such a proposal. I am wondering whether he has given it consideration and whether the government has reached any decision on the matter.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, we have been considering the matter. It is not a subject which lends itself to easy investigation and dogmatic conclusions, but officials of the government are making that kind of investigation now.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext: A supplementary question. I know it is hard to decide when this study would be available, but can the Prime Minister give us any indication of the likely length of time which would be involved?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext: I should think it would not be possible to produce any results which would have any real significance in a matter of this kind before the autumn.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a most interesting situation. The government of Canada has civil servants giving consideration to the effects of separatism, or the separation of our country. Would he let the house in on the secret as to what is the nature of the authority for this? What are these people supposed to investigate? This is a most unusual thing, for the government of Canada to engage in such a procedure.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if it were unusual then it is surprising that the right hon. gentleman did not rise to express his surprise when the matter came up two or three weeks ago.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext: I thought the answer you gave then was ridiculous.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Now the right hon. gentleman is quite disturbed about this. What is being undertaken is an economic investigation of the interrelation between Quebec and the rest of the country, which is surely a very proper subject for an economic investigation.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext: That was not the answer given to the hon. member who asked the question. The answer given was that a study was being made of the problems arising out of separation, as I recall it. The Prime Minister says he is surprised that I am concerned about this. I am concerned that the government would be considering a proposal like ;hat.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext: I am very surprised that the right hon. gentleman tried to draw political conclusions from this.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext: No, but this is the most surprising thing I have ever heard.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC  AGREEMENT RESPECTING STUDENT LOANS AND FAMILY ALLOWANCES

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC  AGREEMENT RESPECTING STUDENT LOANS AND FAMILY ALLOWANCES
speechtext: A supplementary question. Can the Prime Minister tell us whether agreement has been reached with all the provinces except Quebec, or can he tell us with how many provinces he has reached agreement.

speechtext: No. There are one or two provinces which are anxious to have further information in this latter matter regarding some of the details of the administration of the scheme, but we hope this will all be cleared up within a few days.

Mr. Chairman, the President of the Privy Council is going to give us some information with respect to the secretaries in ministers' offices outside the Ottawa-Hull area. I think he said yesterday that there were 15 full-time persons and one part-time person located outside Ottawa. I asked him last night to tell us where they are located and in how many instances they are located in the actual constituency of the minister in question.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would be very glad to give that information, Mr. Chairman. Hon. members will appreciate that so far as the President of the Privy Council is concerned his whole department is located in Ottawa, and all his staff is located in his own constitutency. Therefore I will interpret the remarks as being related only to staff outside the immediate Ottawa-Hull area. There is some uncertainty in my mind as to which constituency the Vancouver office is in, so if I just give the Vancouver city office perhaps that will be sufficient, because I was not able to verify the physical location of the building within the constituency. Subject to that reservation and my remarks yesterday about Mr. Cote, the following is what I deem to be an accurate and precise list.
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, in the public immigration building at Quebec city, one employee; the Minister of Fisheries at Bathurst in a private place, not a public building, one employee.
Where?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Bathurst, New Brunswick.
Is that in the minister's constituency?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is either in or very close to it. I will get the information for the hon. member.
It is in his riding.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am told it is in his constituency. The Minister of Industry and

Defence Production, one employee, clerk, grade 1, at Montreal in a public building.
In the constituency?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, I believe not. The Minister of Justice, one employee in Montreal, not in the constituency; the Minister of National Defence, one employee in a public building, not in the constituency.
Where?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In Toronto. The Associate Minister of National Defence, two employees at Sorel in the constituency; the Minister of National Health and Welfare, one employee in the constituency; the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, two employees at Vancouver, not in the constituency.
In the same city?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes. The Postmaster
General, two employees in Vancouver. I am not certain whether the actual office is in the constituency or outside it. I will try to verify that. The Minister of Public Works, two employees in Montreal, not in the constituency; the Secretary of State, one employee in Montreal, not in the constituency; the Minister of Veterans Affairs, one employee in the constituency. That employee is only a part time employee at a salary of $2,000 a year. In case anyone asks about the order in council, there is an assistant indicated in the order in council as being in the minister's constituency but I And on investigation that in fact he lives in the immediate Ottawa-Hull area and is in fact in Ottawa. I mention that in case someone reads the order in council. I believe that list to be full and precise.

May I ask the minister this question? We have knowledge of two orders in council now and in the case of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration the employee working in the office of the minister is described in the order in council as being at Baie des Sables. The minister says that he is actually in Ottawa most of the time. Now he tells us that another employee described in the order in council as working in the constituency is actually located here.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not know that it is fair to say that in the order in council they are described as working in the constituency. In any event, in the one case the man has never worked in the particular town or village of Baie des Sables although he has worked parttime in the constituency. That is the point I am making. The practice in drafting the

orders in council has varied over the years. If you go back for 30 years checking through the orders in council, as I have tried to do to unearth information, it is obvious that they do not give the whole record, although they are perfectly effective and proper orders in council. There are changes in the form of setting them up which does make it quite difficult, and in fairness to hon. members I thought I should point out these two cases. In the case of the order in council referring to Baie des Sables, this man works here mostly, and also in the constituency, but never in the particular village referred to in the order in council.
With regard to the other case, if you read the order in council you will see that he is said to be working at a particular place in the constituency. In fact, he lives in the immediate Ottawa-Hull area and works in Ottawa. It is true that he does go to the constituency occasionally. Incidentally, I found no travelling expenses for him, which pleased me very much. I wanted to make these precautionary remarks in case the orders in council are subsequently turned up and appear to indicate that something I have said is not precisely accurate. I believe what I have said to be precise and accurate and it certainly represents an attempt to get at the problem in a very full way.

Mr. Chairman, to me the minister's statement is far from satisfactory. He says that the individual mentioned in the order in council, Mr. Andre Cot6, is most of the time in Ottawa but he also does some work in the constituency and in that event is located at Baie des Sables.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, not in that case. That is the point I am making. This is the third time I have made the point. He is never at Baie des Sables. There is no office at Baie des Sables. So far as I can find out he has never been at Baie des Sables in his working hours since he was appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Precisely. That is the very point I was trying to make. Here is an order in council obviously prepared to cover a man who came from the village of Baie des Sables and somebody put his address in because they found out he was going to do some work in the constituency. I came forward frankly and told the house what the situation was. Baie des Sables, which unfortunately I have never seen, is a relatively small community. But it is the home of this man whence he came when he was employed by the minister. I have looked at the map to satisfy myself, and I am told that when he goes to the constituency he does not go to this smaller community or centre. He goes to the main centres of population in the constituency, such as Matane. Incidentally, he was in the gallery when these questions were asked some days ago and he is in the gallery today. He is based at Ottawa and operates in Ottawa, but he does go to the constituency from time to time.

This is exactly the point. I am not concerned about what he does in the minister's office in Ottawa. I am concerned about the fact that apparently there are employees paid out of the public treasury who are located in the constituencies of ministers. In the case of Andre Cote apparently he is here part of the time and in the constituency part of the time. I want to know what he does in the constituency. Apparently the Minister of Fisheries has someone at Bathurst in his constituency. The Associate Minister of National Defence has two people at Sorel in his constituency. With respect to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the order in council I have only covers one person in her constituency although I thought the President of the Privy Council said there were two.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, one.

One in Niagara Falls, then, and it says in the order in council appointing this person that she is to be located at Niagara Falls. The Minister of Veterans Affairs has someone part-time in St. Boniface.
Now, Mr. Chairman, no one is contesting the minister's right to have someone in his office where he is doing government business. However, the whole defence put up by

Interim Supply
the President of the Privy Council yesterday was, first, that this thing has been done for many years, which seems to me to be no argument at all. He said, in fact, they have improved upon the practice of the past because now these orders in council appointing these persons who are in ministers' constituencies are subject to review from time to time by the treasury board.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, that is not the way he put it.
I believe the minister said the treasury board reviewed these from time to time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.
Do I understand they are not reviewed at all?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, you do not understand it.
They are approved by the treasury board, then an order in council is passed and there is no review from time to time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I did not say that. It seems that throughout the proceedings today the hon. member has rather lost track of what I did say yesterday. I had undertaken to get information for the hon. member and discuss this matter on interim supply. As I pointed out in the early part of my remarks, this was a practice going back many years. I indicated how far back, but I have not tried to check just how far back it goes. I know it goes back as far as 1935, but I have no idea how many years before that.
I said that the practice was the same as that which had been in existence under the former government. There was one slight change and that was that treasury board had to deal with the recommendations before they were brought forward under section 71 for appointment by the governor in council. It is a small change, but it does give treasury board a chance to get at this thing. I then gave a statement in general terms and concluded with these words, which I should like to quote from page 4742 of Hansard:
I must add, Mr. Chairman, that the Prime Minister has instructed the treasury board to examine into the whole question oi ministerial assistants working outside Ottawa. He has asked treasury board to report on how this practice, as it has developed over the years, can be brought under strict control so that abuses, if any, can be prevented, and whether there are any advantages to the public service under the practice which should be retained under the control referred to.

Now, it will be seen at a glance that if you take a country the size of ours the work will be spread out over a vast area. Perhaps I could pick out one city by way of illustration because I have had a chance to look a bit at the work being done in Vancouver. If the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam views the information I have given him he will find that there are three stenographers and one clerk in Vancouver. If you follow the practice of business people in that province, and their habit of communicating with the government or making appointments with ministers and that sort of thing, you will find you have to make a careful evaluation of the situation because it will be seen that keeping these stenographers there, at the regular stenographer's salary, undoubtedly saves a great deal of money to the public treasury. I must confess that when I see the size of the budget deficits, both past and present, that is a source of concern. It is a much better way of getting effective service for the population and the business people who will likely be communicating with the government than closing up the office and having all the staff here. Then, you would have to pay travelling expenses, and if you start travelling the vast mileages necessary in this country, the cost can be very high.
I have picked on Vancouver to illustrate a point. We have the same kind of situation to a limited extent in Winnipeg. There has been an office there for a great many years. In Montreal there has been a public works office in a public building, and I find that they probably do even more work than the minister's staff should be doing. It may well be that they are doing work for the departmental staff as well.
About all I can say that is really effective is that the Prime Minister has issued these instructions and the treasury board are doing precisely what is indicated. They are making a thorough examination of this whole matter to see what abuses, if any, exist. Of course it follows that appropriate action will be taken if any do exist. It will be seen this is not a simple matter of just having everybody work in Ottawa. This is no solution at all to the problem. When some questions were asked some time ago on orders of the day, the inference was-I must say I made a note of it very quickly-that these persons were doing other than ministerial work in the local constituencies at the constituency level. If that were the case it would, of course, be objectionable. I do not find that is so. We have a proposition here. The ministers are

expected to produce results and I think I can say, in all modesty, that they are paid to look after the national business of the country. There is a good deal of work done for ministers to leave them free to deal with public business with which they might otherwise have to deal, or be expected to deal themselves. This matter requires careful evaluation and examination.

The minister has a great capacity for muddying the waters. I started by saying that the minister's argument consisted of two parts: First, in saying that this practice had been going on for some time and that this government was trying to tighten it by having such appointments first of all reviewed by the treasury board prior to appointment. He also said the Prime Minister had asked for a further examination to see if there were any abuses. This really does not satisfy me. A review by the treasury board, a board made up by ministers themselves in the main, regarding the activities of other ministers of the same political party is not going to produce very much by way of careful scrutiny of these appointments.
Now, the other case made by the minister yesterday was that this section 71, subsection (1) of the Civil Service Act under which these appointments are made is being interpreted as meaning, when it says "persons to be employed in the office of the minister shall be appointed by the governor in council", not the place but the function of the minister. This means stretching one's credulity almost to the breaking point.
The President of the Privy Council said he had an opinion from the Minister of Justice on this. I keep wondering whether it was an off the cuff opinion which the minister gave one day after lunch or whether it was a written opinion from his department. I would certainly enjoy seeing it. But even if the minister's interpretation is right, and this office of the minister referred to in the act is not the actual office, the actual room or rooms where the minister's staff may be located, but is the function of the minister, then I still maintain that these appointments are only to assist the minister in carrying out his functions.
To what extent do the ministers' functions as a minister extend to having someone in Sorel, Baie des Sables and Niagara Falls? I am not talking about the minister's function as a member of parliament. The section does not give the governor in council the
Interim Supply
power to appoint staff to do their work as M.P.'s, but to do their work as ministers.
Last night when explaining this to the committee the President of the Privy Council said:
It may well be that ministers could be relieved of much of their obligation to deal with the manifold problems of their constituents by a secretary or a stenographer living in their constituency-
Surely, Mr. Chairman, the function of the minister does not extend to looking after his constituents. That is his function as a member of parliament, and any staff which he requires to look after his constituents and his constituency business is his responsibility, just as it is that of any other member of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Do you pay your secretary?
I pay any secretary I keep in my constituency.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Is it not a fact that every member of the house, whether on the treasury benches or otherwise, is provided with at least one secretary, paid from the public purse, whose responsibilities include looking after constituency matters, correspondence, and anything related to the individual member's constituency, and that those duties are performed with respect to the riding, here in Ottawa and could just as easily be performed in the constituencies?

Mr. Chairman, every member is entitled to secretarial assistance, and the ministers in carrying out their constituency affairs are no different from any other members. When a minister is given the privilege of having a secretary in Niagara Falls-and I refer to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, since she has raised this matter- and the secretary is paid a salary of $5,220, which is much higher than any private member's secretary gets, not to work in Ottawa but to work in Niagara Falls then this is something which is not granted to any other member.
I want to know, is that secretary looking after the work of the department. If so, what public health department work is there in the city of Niagara Falls that this secretary is discharging? The fact is very clear that this person is not doing work for the department. This secretary is looking after the affairs of the minister, not in her capacity as a minister of the crown but in her capacity as a member of parliament. But if any of the rest of us need secretarial help in our

Interim Supply
constituencies we expect to supply it ourselves, and we do.
What 1 am quarrelling with is that an order in council, passed under a section
which gives the government the right to appoint secretarial staff or other staff to work for a minister, is restricted to the minister in his or her function as a minister of the crown, and does not give the governor in council power to appoint persons to work in a minister's constituency to do tasks which are related to the minister's responsibility as a member of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit another question? Is it not a fact that work done in Ottawa, work done in Niagara Falls or Burnaby-Coquitlam, being of the same type and being done by an individual counting off against an establishment is exactly similar in kind? Is it not also a fact that the hon. member, who is concerned over this matter, has on his staff a number of individuals who are paid from the public purse, one in particular a Mr. Pope who frequently does work for his member outside of Ottawa, and yet his salary is paid at public expense?

May I ask a question of the minister? If what she says is correct then I take it there is no difference between her operation of the department in her own constituency and in my constituency in Vancouver. If so, does she intend to appoint somebody in my riding in Vancouver and, if not, why is it only in her constituency where this appointment is made?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I will be happy-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam had the floor and when he has concluded we might continue with questions.

The minister's question simply points up the whole problem so far as the government and the committee are concerned, that either the staff which the public pays for should be available in members' constituencies or should be restricted to Ottawa, and it should be the same for everybody. But if the ministers are going to have staff working in their constituencies they ought not to be appointed under section 71. They ought to be appointed in their capacity as members of parliament. This section however only gives the governor in council power to appoint persons to help a minister discharge his or her responsibility as a minister of the crown and not as a mem-

ber of parliament, and I think that this can lead to a great deal of abuse.
If the government wants to adopt something of the system they have in England, of allowing members to have agents, and paying them to look after the business of the members in their constituencies, that is a policy which could well be considered; but the government has not followed that policy. What I and others are afraid of is that by a back door method, of appointing people under the pretext that they are helping a minister carry out his ministerial duties, this is actually being used to appoint people to carry out constituency duties, and this borders on political duties. This is a very serious matter and the fact that it has gone on some time does not excuse it at all. I hope we get some satisfactory explanation as to whether the government is going to continue this practice, is going to extend it, or is going to discontinue it.
For instance, the minister said that when a minister of the crown goes to a city it is useful to have someone to make appointments. I quite agree that when a minister goes back to Vancouver undoubtedly organizations and individuals will want to see him in his ministerial capacity, but I cannot believe that among all the civil servants a minister has in Vancouver, Toronto or Montreal, there is not someone who can look after his appointments without having a secretary located there full-time to deal with the one or two days a month that he may be in the city.
I hope the government will not allow this thing to drift into serious abuse. I for one am quite dissatisfied with the explanations that have been given. I am convinced that what is being done now improperly, under the guise of appointing staff to do ministerial duties, is actually appointing staff to carry on constituency work. If the government is going to give ministers constituency agents, and make ministers different from other members of parliament, then it should come out and say so. If it is going to give similar staff to all members of parliament, then it should announce that policy; but I do not think it should rely on the subterfuge of appointing people under section 71(1) and having them do constituency work.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I wish to answer one point raised by the hon. gentleman. He made reference to civil servants doing the type of work done by the staff in Vancouver-I refer to Vancouver because I had the opportunity of learning about the situation there. I would

be the very first to object if we got into a position where civil servants were the ones who were telephoning to Ottawa for appointments to get ministers to go here, there, and everywhere in that province, making appointments for the people of that province to see ministers in that area, and passing on correspondence to them. I hope he did not mean to imply in the course of his remarks that civil servants should be all mixed up with the minister's staff, and vice-versa. I hope we are on common ground in this regard and that on reflection he will agree with me on this point, at least, because I do not think he could have realized the implications in his remarks.
There is one other point which the hon. gentleman raised-a general point which seems to be based on a wrong premise. It is a fact of geography in this country that our ministers come from most of the provinces of Canada. I regret I am compelled to say "most provinces" instead of "all provinces". In any event, the point I am making is that, though they represent the whole country as ministers in the cabinet, the fact of life is that they do come from a particular province and are looked on in those areas as the provincial minister, or the area minister, in the federal cabinet. Because in some cases a particular office is located in a town in the constituency of a minister, rather than in some other town in the region is, surely, no reason why the inference must be drawn from this fact alone that the person concerned is doing constituency work.
What are they doing?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is the point. We are checking right through, as I told the hon. member. And, as I was careful to say in the concluding part of my remarks, the Prime Minister has given instructions-
Tell us what their duties are now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think I can do that. The hon. gentleman was premier of a province and I have a suspicion-in fact, I have more than a suspicion-that he used the minister's staff outside the city of Regina. He knows that.
Would the minister be specific? Is that a statement or an hypothesis? Give us particulars.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes. When I was solicitor for the province-I think I could check up the records; I will give them.

The minister need not be coy. If he has any charge to make, I want him to make it. If not, he should withdraw it.

speechtext: I have no charge to make whatever. The point I am making is this-
The minister is dancing away from this and I will not allow it. The minister made a statement. He will either substantiate it or withdraw it. He dances away from almost everything he has been asked.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Perhaps I might be allowed to withdraw-
I have the floor, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: My understanding is that the minister has the floor.

The minister has danced away from almost everything he has been asked, but he is not going to dance away from this. He will now either substantiate what he said, or withdraw it. Or he will tell me he is making a hypothesis, and if he does I will want confirmation of that.

speechtext: The hon. member has taken the time to put on the record some further observations which are unnecessary. I did withdraw it. How many times does he want me to withdraw?

Slander.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will tell the hon. gentleman. For instance, I sent a member of my staff to Kingston some days ago to undertake certain work of a rather technical nature which I regard pretty much as my own concern. That is the point I was trying to make.

The matter before us now concerns an appointment to a minister's office in a constituency. I certainly heard an allegation made that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, a former premier of a province, did the same thing.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I never made any such statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I may say in any event, whether the statement was made or not, whatever statement was made by the minister, he withdrew it, and I suggest that this particular incident be forgotten. I should like to call on the hon. member for Medicine Hat who has been wanting to speak for a while.
I think perhaps because the leader of the New Democratic party-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am wondering whether we should not give an opportunity now to other members who have been trying to get into this debate. They would like to say a word, and I suggest we recognize the hon. member for Medicine Hat.

There are one or two matters I should like to place before some of the ministers opposite. I wish to ask the ministers who have requested treasury board to make these appointments providing for

people to work in their constituencies just what, in fact, these people are doing.
I think the argument advanced a few minutes ago by the Minister of National Health and Welfare is tantamount to an admission that they are in fact doing constituency business. The hon. lady tried to argue that all members have the privilege of hiring a secretary to take on their constituency business in Ottawa. I drew the inference that this was justification for her having an appointment made under this section of the act by treasury board of someone in her constituency to take on her constituency business. I want the President of the Privy Council and the ministers who have made these appointments to know that no member of this House of Commons, as far as I know, has the privilege of having a secretary to attend to his constituency business anywhere except in his office in Ottawa. We would like to know whether or not this is the case, because it just so happens that the secretary who is on the staff of the House of Commons here in Ottawa and is assigned to my office did in fact go to the constituency of Medicine Hat during the Christmas recess and was there until some time in February, and during that period she was not paid by the House of Commons. If there are members of this house, be they ministers or otherwise, who are enjoying the privilege of having secretaries paid to attend to constituency business in their constituencies, I think this practice should either be extended to all members or withdrawn.
The President of the Privy Council has attempted to muddy the waters, as has been pointed out, and stick-handle this question which has been put to him a number of times; but so far we have not received any clear explanation from the Minister of Veterans Affairs, the Minister of National Health and Welf are or the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration as to the exact duties these people are performing. We all know very well that the Minister of National Health and Welfare, for example, has an office in Ottawa. We know there is an office of this department in Toronto, in Winnipeg, in Regina, in Edmonton and in British Columbia; and we also know-

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the hon. member would not want to mislead the committee. There is no office of a minister in Winnipeg. There is only one office for the province of Manitoba, and that happens to be in St. Boniface, at the moment, in the public post office.
I said there was an office, or a branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare, in Winnipeg.
And in St. Boniface.

And perhaps in St. Boniface. Anyway, Mr. Chairman, there are a number of them all across the country. Members of this house have no objection whatever to ministers using the staff of this house to assist them in their function as minister of whatever department it happens to be. But these three cases of appointments by treasury board of other staff in the constituency appear to me to have nothing to do with their function as ministers of the crown.
With regard to the argument advanced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, to the effect that she is entitled to this kind of person on her staff in Niagara Falls because other members of the House of Commons have the right to hire a secretary to attend to constituency business, I think she is entirely wrong because the premise of that argument is false. Members of this house do not have that privilege, and I have personal [DOT]experience to buttress that argument. Therefore I think if we are to get at the heart of this question, which is a very valid one, we should have an explanation from these three ministers at least as to just exactly what these three people do in their constituencies while they are being paid by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am very 3iappy to have the opportunity to speak on this matter; I have been waiting for it all afternoon. In the first place, I should like to say to the committee that I am not being [DOT]defensive-I do not intend to be-and I deny any allegation that there is any subterfuge or anything wrong in what I have done I am speaking of what I myself have done as Minister of National Health and Welfare and I should like the committee to know "this.
Within a day or so of my appointment to this portfolio I was advised of the size of the establishment of the minister's office. Some individuals had been employed by my predecessor, and remained; some left of their volition a few days before this government took office. Some of those individuals had been appointed by Mr. Martin, who was my predecessor's predecessor. They perform different jobs, and the establishment was set up, I presume, by the civil service commission. [DOT]Some of them are what members of parliament would call regular civil servants; that is, they have come up through the civil
Interim Supply
service and have moved into the ministerial staff. Some of them have been appointed to the ministerial staff or have taken the civil service examination in the past and have come into the staff. We have everything from messengers up to the most qualified senior clerks in the ministerial offices.
Every member of the House of Commons has at least one individual appointed to his staff here in the house. Admittedly this is while the session is on. That individual is appointed and is paid from public funds for one purpose, obviously, namely to deal with the member's constituency work. A minister of the crown has no sessional staff over and above those individuals allotted to him or her as members of the ministerial staff.
Obviously the work which a minister carries on also involves that of a member of parliament, and he or she is as entitled to a staff member to carry out this work as any other member of parliament. It should be remembered that more than one half of the remuneration of a minister of the crown is paid for being a member of parliament. This work must be completed, but no individual is appointed to ministers' staffs for sessional purposes at all.
The discussion has not been heated today, but there has been a faint suggestion by hon. members of sticking one's fingers in the till. I deny such an allegation. The practice, rightly or wrongly, has been going on for 30 years. Civil servants have informed me of it and I imagine that the same thing has happened with my colleagues. Our senior civil servants informed us, when we took over the responsibilities of the department, of the way in which the minister's office was operated. There was absolutely no reason for any of us to inquire into whether there was anything wrong in it, just as there was no reason to inquire into any other information we were given.
We had information as to how our predecessors operated. In my particular case my predecessor did not establish an office in his own constituency; instead he had to appoint people whom he was entitled to have, namely an executive secretary and an executive assistant. This was done by a great many ministers. In particular I remember that it was done by Mr. Fulton as minister of justice. Those individuals, instead of appointing someone to their constituency office had a rather high priced man, in some cases with a salary of $9,000 a year or more, flying back and forth to the constituency. Their expense accounts were charged to the public purse.

Interim Supply
They were doing the minister's work in and out of the constituency.
In my own view, to have someone who is a clerk, who is a contact not only for me as a member in my constituency but perhaps, more importantly, for me as the minister for southern Ontario, for something in excess of 5 million people, most of whom through their members or otherwise contact me in my constituency-presumably to save themselves the cost of long distance travel and long distance telephone calls-is a necessity.
Like the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquit-lam and every other member in this house, I have great pride in being a good constituency man. I have always tried to take a great deal of care of my people. Since I have been appointed as a minister of the crown I have found, particularly because of pressures regarding pension legislation, that it has been virtually impossible to be in my constituency. Accordingly I have done what a great many other members do, and that is put on a telephone answering service 24 hours a day and run up long distance telephone bills at my own expense in telephoning back and forth to my constituents. But there has been no way of having personal contact with people, not just from the riding of Niagara Falls, which constitutes 80,000 people and for which I am paid $18,000 a year for being their member, but also all the people from southern Ontario who wish to get in touch with me as the minister for the area. Surely every member realizes that a minister does not just have the responsibility of an individual portfolio but has also the responsibility of a member of parliament representing these people.
In addition to that, because of my particular portfolio a great deal of work is generated regarding pensions, family allowances and matters of that kind by individuals all over the country. Many of these people are not literate in either the French or English language. Accordingly, I ask them to come to the office; I want that to be clear. This office is established in a public building. As far as I know there has never been one similar in my constituency, although my constituency was formerly represented by a minister of labour, Mr. Humphrey Mitchell. At this time his executive assistant was sent to the constituency. I remember his staying at a hotel for a week at a time at public expense arranging for people in that area to see the minister. Therefore I know from my own knowledge that this is a practice which has gone on for more than 30 years.

Hon. members have said that they do not have this kind of privilege. It was not very long ago that I was a private member, and I am well aware that there are differences between the privileges and responsibilities of members of the privy council and those of individual private members. If there were not those difference I would not imagine that too many members on that side would want to get over to this side and sit on the front benches. But with parliament sitting eight to ten months a year now we who in this house are not only members of the executive branch but members of the legislative branch are incapable of looking after our primary responsibility for which purpose we were elected, and for which purpose we are paid, namely constituency work.
I should just like to put my position on record. Each of my colleagues may have a quite different position, but if I were to represent, as did my hon. friend opposite, the wonderful province of Manitoba, and had a constituency office in Brandon, or if I were to represent Nova Scotia-I am not certain whether the former minister of finance had one too, but I think he did-and I represented the whole province of Nova Scotia or Manitoba, I would be happy to have such an office and would feel that the people of that province would be better served by the minister from the province if there were such an office.
The hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam suggested that this was political. I think too often members of parliament sneer at that word. But I can say on my honour as a member of the House of Commons that no piece of patronage work, no political work in that sense, has ever been performed in this office. Although I was informed about a year ago that I was able to open such an office I did not do so until this spring, when it became perfectly apparent that no matter how work was arranged here in Ottawa with reference to the individuals in southern Ontario, and more particularly in my constituency, their needs could not be attended to properly. Yet in setting up such an office my staff was advised never to ask the politics of anyone who came in the door. The sign on the door says: "Department of National Health and Welfare Minister's Office". The stationery used in that office is the stationery which is used in each of the several offices I have, also in Ottawa. When I am in my constituency I work physically in that office, and outside it sits the secretary at her desk, as the receptionist. I suspect that if there is a summer recess I

will be working in that office every day. When I am in my constituency I expect that I will be handling not only constituency work but also departmental work as minister in Ottawa.
If this type of practice is improper and illegal I should like to know, because I have no desire to do anything which is improper and illegal. I would appeal to the hon. members of the house not to suggest that simply because this sort of thing has been done there is something underhanded, that subterfuge has been used. This practice has been carried on for quite a time, as I have pointed out, in different ways in different constituencies. There was no attempt to hide the fact in the order in council that this individual was going to work in Niagara Falls, and my constituency was in fact informed about it in speeches, by telephone calls and in every way possible, and the public invited to come to the office. Liaison has been arranged with the provincial welfare and the municipal welfare people, who move in and out of the office in an attempt to serve the people in the area.
If I have done wrong, if section 71 does not, as I believe it does, extend to appointing someone in the office of the minister to do the work of the minister, if this is improper I shall at once discharge her and close this office. I do not believe there is anything improper in that which I have done, and with respect, Mr. Chairman, I do not believe that the members of the committee will find anything improper or that there is any subterfuge involved.
Mr. Chairman, I just want to take one moment, if I may, to try and explain the value of this kind of arrangement as far as Manitoba is concerned.
I do not know whether my hon. friend is making a maiden speech, but I have the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I did call on the Minister of Veterans Affairs.

I simply wish to say that as far as Manitoba is concerned I have found it essential, and all my predecessors from that province have found it essential, that there be an office in that province available to the public, to all the citizens of the province, where they can talk to someone and find a means of getting information from the minister, from his department and from other departments of government.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not have one. Why did you say all your predecessors had one? Let us be accurate about this.
I beg the hon. member's pardon.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You said all your predecessors maintained an office with a staff there. I did not and I was one of your predecessors in the Department of Veterans Affairs.

Then I apologize to the hon. gentleman. My information was that one existed in the general post office building in Winnipeg, and instead of using that I opened one in the general post office in St. Boniface. I did this in order to serve the people of that area, because I feel it is important. Otherwise it would mean that someone from my office would occasionally have to travel to Manitoba, and the net cost involved here represents a saving. This office is open to serve the public. I would feel very badly if we had to make a change because I think it is useful to the public of Manitoba.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question. I understand that there is a district office of the Department of Veterans Affairs in Winnipeg. Is that not so?
Yes.
What do they do in the minister's personal office which cannot be handled by the federal office located in Winnipeg?

This is a question of the office being located in St. Boniface rather than Winnipeg. I think there is a good reason for that office to be occasionally located there instead of on the other side of the river, otherwise it would not be accessible to the people there. There is a distinction in going to the Department of Veterans Affairs, where there is a considerable amount of traffic.

speechtext: Shall I call it five o'clock?

Subject to the feelings of the house, this matter concerns such a serious misuse of the statute that if it could be cleared up within the hour I would be content to relinquish my right to speak on my bill, and have it listed for some day next week.

May I suggest that a decision on this point be made with the Speaker in the chair.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the remarks of the hon. member for Danforth I wonder whether the house would grant permission to continue with interim supply from five to six?
I am quite agreeable to that, provided it is understood that my bill will be called in the first hour next week.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It will not lose its position, there having been no private members' hour.
I am agreeable to that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it agreed that we will suspend private members' hour?
Agreed.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Veterans Affairs. May I say with all respect, or perhaps disrespect, that it is not possible to accept their statements. How can they hope to bamboozle members of the House of Commons and expect that we are so naive as to accept what they have said?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: On a question of personal privilege, is the member saying he does not accept what I have said?
I said that you cannot expect us to be so naive as to accept what you have said.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Is the member saying he does not accept my word as a member of the House of Commons?

I accept your word, but not what has happened. If one, two or three cabinet ministers have found it necessary to make special appointments by means of a recommendation by treasury board approved by the governor general in council in order for them to discharge their responsibilities as ministers holding the portfolios of health and welfare, immigration and veterans affairs, may I ask how it is that the other 17 cabinet ministers have not yet found it necessary to carry on their business in the same way? If, for example, such appointment is for immigration purposes, will we finally find out how many landed immigrants have been processed through the office in the minister's riding and how many immigration cases there are in the minister's constituency? I am getting on very well without the minister rising and I want to deal with this matter on this basis.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare comes from Niagara Falls, a particular area in Ontario. Why is it that it is not important for her to have a representative in the other 264 constituencies of Canada? May I ask why the Minister of Veterans Affairs requires a representative in his constituency? I am usually pretty honest and not naive. These appointments by cabinet ministers are political appointments for party patronage purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is not true.

There cannot be any other answer. I was most interested in what the Minister of National Health and Welfare said a few minutes ago about her responsibilities and how she had to have somebody in her riding able to approach people and report to her. She said that we as members of the House of Commons have secretaries. Of course we have when the house is in session. I admit that as a minister she cannot get back to her riding very often. We all admit that. But I cannot go back the 3,000 miles to my riding of Vancouver East either. As a matter of fact I think my attend-

ance in the house is close to a record. I have only lost three full days since February 18. My riding of Vancouver East is just as important to me as the Liberal riding of the minister is to her. She made a statement-I am sorry, I should say that the minister made a statement because you should not call a minister a she.
You would not call her a he.
I would not call her a he. As a matter of fact, I should like to know about the invitation to marriage because 1 read that she would like to become a mother.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Really, Mr. Chairman, I do not know to what my hon. friend refers. However, not only do I think that I deserve some respect as a woman from him but also my office deserves some respect. I have no idea what the reference he has just made means, but I do ask him to realize that he is speaking in the highest court in the land, that there are children in the galleries, and that the few reporters in the press gallery who understand English may occasionally read Hansard and produce reports for the public press. Therefore I ask him at least to pay attention to what he is saying.

Mr. Chairman, whether I am in the highest court of the land or the lowest court of the land I always honour women. My point is that the minister said that with all her staff she had no one to take care of her constituency business. That was the implication. Am I correct? The minister acknowledges that I am correct. If that is so, how does she think that members of the house take care of their constituency business when they do not have the authority to appoint anybody in their constituencies?
Let ministers as well as members be honest. These appointments were made by these cabinet ministers at government expense for strictly political purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is not so.

If not, then there should be an office of the department, not the political party, in the ridings where these appointments have been made. In the constituencies of each of the three cabinet ministers and in the towns that have been named, where is there an official office under the control of the cabinet minister for the carrying on of government business which requires the appointment of somebody representing the minister in that constituency with a salary ranging from $5,000 to $7,500 a year?
Interim Supply
The cabinet ministers concerned can make all the explanations they like. This is still political patronage for the maintenance of party control in their own constituencies. There is no other basis for these appointments. There is no other reason for these appointments, and they are completely against the laws and regulations of parliament. I hope that the time will come when greater consideration will be given to the needs of members as well as cabinet ministers.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I do want to say this, that the real meaning of government is honesty; the real meaning of democracy is following the principle that what is right for one is right for all. The government is a minority. It can carry on if it conducts the business of the people. It can carry on also if it does not make a farce of the rules and regulations. All three ministers concerned are fairly close to their constituencies, but there are about 150 of us in this house who are a lot farther away from our ridings. There are a number of us who have not been back to our constituencies, except for three days or a week, since February 18.
If a cabinet minister can say that because of responsibilities he needs somebody in his own riding, appointed by subterfuge at government expense, then other members have that right and privilege, too. Until you are prepared to be absolutely honest and give rights to all members, to recognize the distances in Canada, then I say that the three appointments made, irrespective of everything said by the three ministers, are political, constituency appointments for political control of their own organizations in their ridings and not for the work covered by their positions as cabinet ministers.

I wanted to ask the minister if he could give me the duties of these people. I find it very strange, for example, that in the city of Toronto we have an assistant to the Minister of National Defence, yet the more important cabinet posts of trade and commerce and finance do not seem to require that type of assistance. I know the minister is a bit uncomfortable at this apparent misuse of the statute, but I want to say to him in the beginning that it is not particularly helpful to the discussion for him to make the type of innuendo against the leader of our party that he did a little while ago. I can understand the uncomfortable nature of his position, but I do not think it is helpful to make that kind of innuendo and then try to withdraw it, because the innuendo is in the record.

Interim Supply
It is a rather unfortunate thing that he would try to sidetrack it in that way.
I do not want to go through the whole list of these appointments, but really we have had no satisfactory answer at all on this subject. We still do not know what these people are doing for their ministers in their capacity as ministers, over and above the duties of the minister as a private member. All of us have sympathy for the ministers. They have a great deal of work to do and they would like to have some assistance in their ridings, but you cannot do it in this back door method. You are misusing this statute. I would not go quite as far as saying the appointments are illegal, but certainly I should like to see the whole matter referred to the courts for an interpretation. I doubt very much if the wording of the statute, which is quite clear in its provision that these people are to work in the minister's office, can be stretched to appoint people in constituencies. By the admission of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, this assistant is dealing with business on a constituency basis.
It is really fatuous to suggest that the reason for the appointment is that the minister represents all of southern Ontario. I am sure every member of the house can say, as I can, that I receive correspondence from members of our party in various constituencies across the country. It is a ridiculous argument to say that because she is the minister for all of southern Ontario this is required. We are simply not satisfied with the explanation. We want to know what justification there is for this type of misuse of a public statute. We have not received any information at all from the President of the Privy Council or from the other ministers who have spoken that would in any way justify the conduct in this case. I suggest that until you do give us proper answers we want to sit here and talk about it. The alternatives are either, (a) refer this matter to the court for a ruling as to whether you can make use of a statute in this way or (b) rescind these appointments until such time as you can satisfy the House of Commons that the procedure you are adopting is legal and proper.
After all, it is our historic right to insist that public funds be spent in a constitutional and proper manner. Nothing you have said today has convinced us that you are following a proper course. It is not sufficient to tell us that this practice has been followed by previous administration. I understand that in the case of the present Leader of the Opposition, he stopped this practice when

he was prime minister. The mere fact that this procedure has been used by previous Liberal administrations is not sufficient justification for pursuing it now.
I want to again ask the minister to go through this list of departments. For example, the associate minister of defence has two persons in his constituency. What are they doing for him as minister, over and above his capacity as a private member? The minister of northern affairs has two people in Vancouver. What are they doing there? What are their duties to him as a minister, in a city in which there are regional offices for his department? The Postmaster General has two in Vancouver. What are their duties? What are they doing for him in his capacity as a minister-
Checking to see that the mail arrives.

-as distinct from his capacity as a private member? The Minister of Public Works has two in Montreal, again in his own area. The Secretary of State has one in Montreal. It is just too coincidental, Mr. Chairman, that all these appointments happen to be either in the constituency of the minister involved or in such close proximity to the constituency that it does not really matter.
This is a very serious charge. I would not go quite as far as my colleague who just spoke. I am not suggesting that there is anything deliberately sinister in these appointments, but you simply have not satisfied us. I want to ask the minister again to get up and tell us, as he has not done, what these people are doing in these constituencies. I find it very interesting that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, handling one of the most complex and difficult departments, has not needed an assistant in his constituency. I find it a strange coincidence that the Minister of Finance, carrying perhaps the heaviest portfolio in the city of Toronto, has not seen fit to require such assistance. Again, we want to know, what is it all about? What are these people doing there, because from what has been said today the implication that will go out across the country is that these people are performing duties for ministers in their political capacity or in their capacity as a private member, and for that there is absolutely no legal justification under the section which you have used to make these appointments. I want to give the minister an opportunity to answer.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member has raised several points and I should like to deal very

briefly with one, that is the interpretation of the section. I do not propose to develop the argument I made last night on that. I am convinced of the legality of the appointments, but that is not, I respectfully suggest-
Would the minister read the section so we know what he is discussing?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I must warn the Leader of the Opposition that it is one page in length. This is section 71 of the Civil Service Act. After I satisfied myself, and because the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre had intimated a doubt about the legality, I took the precaution of asking the Minister of Justice for an opinion on it.
Would you table the opinion?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, it is not proper to table such an opinion and it has never been the practice. I think that is elementary. I invite the hon. member for Danforth to read the remainder of subsection 1 of the authority for the appointment. I invite him to continue on reading this section and notice the inter-changability of the use of the words "position" and "office", particularly as it appears in the first part of subsection 2.
Further, if he is familiar with the whole act, I invite him to notice the drawing of the distinction between departmental civil servants, what we would call regular civil servants, and these service sections that deal with publicly paid special employees, drawn from outside the general divisions of the regular civil service. If he does that he will be more satisfied on the legal question.
Now, I do not wish to put this thing on narrow legal grounds, though that is a very important point and I am not in any way underestimating it. But assuming I am right in that, there still remains the larger question on which to be satisfied concerning public funds. I am sorry I am not better able to satisfy the hon. member, but I assure him I had no intention of casting any aspersion on the leader of his party. I was seeking to illustrate the regional nature of the ministers' appointments, and the fact that they have been regarded as regional has gone on so far as I know since confederation.
I was solicitor to that province for a great number of years and, to allay the hon. member's fears a bit more, if I made a reference that was taken up in any way, I immediately withdrew it because I had no intention of casting any aspersion on the hon. member. I was trying to indicate what had not been appreciated, the regional nature of ministers' appointments in this country, and

if the hon. member goes back over Hansard he will see that just before this I had spoken about Vancouver, to illustrate the fact that the provinces regard certain ministers as their ministers, and this is certainly true of the smaller provinces. I made indirect reference to the fact that the government has no minister from Saskatchewan-
The people decided that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That was the sole point I was seeking to raise on that issue, so I hope the hon. member will accept my word on that point, and I think Hansard will bear me out if he looks at it more carefully in the light of what I have said.
Now, coming to the particular point I have made, where I said I would not justify the practice by saying it had been there as far back as I could check, I do not think that is a sufficient answer by itself, but I think if I had not given that information I would have been less than frank with the committee. I do not see how I could do otherwise than give it and that is the reason why I gave it. If hon. members will look at my answer carefully they will see I described it as a practice going on since 1935, and I had illustrated it throughout the years since, but I had certainly not meant that as a full justification of it.
I had then gone on to point out what apparently seems to have missed the attention of the hon. member for Danforth, precisely what we are doing now that this matter has been drawn to our attention; and this was contained in the very last part of my remarks last evening. I thought I made that point clear.
Now, as to the particular offices, I said I had gone through the Vancouver office quite carefully and I sought to illustrate that I was completely satisfied that, whether it is due to the Rocky mountains, or whatever it is, that province regards itself as far away -separated, if you like, in a physical sense, from Ottawa. It is a long distance away, from Ottawa. It is a long distance away, with difficult means of communication, expensive costs of telephone calls and a few things like that. In any event it is the practice of people all over that province to come to that office, which is staffed with relatively junior staff, to make appointments and get information about business at Ottawa, a great deal of it by way of information as to where this or that should be directed. I fully satisfied myself on that office because I had an opportunity of getting through it, and I had satis-
