fied myself that there was no work of a local party nature in that office.
With respect to what has been said about the office in Winnipeg, I would draw the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that the province of Manitoba seems to feel some pride-and I share that pride-in the fact that it is a province of some considerable substance and there is, and always has been, a minister's office maintained in that province.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: But not a minister's assistant in that office.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre would just mind checking that statement before he leaves it on Hansard. I would draw the attention of the hon. member for Danforth to the fact that this employee in the St. Boniface office is drawing the magnificent salary of $2,000 a year, with no travel expenses of any kind, and I invite-
What does that prove?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It proves I have some responsibility for financing this country's expenditures and if I am satisfied that employee is doing proper work in the minister's office relating to the minister's duties, I am not going to cut off that $2,000 to be replaced by an expenditure of many more thousands of dollars for travel expenses and that sort of thing.
The minister is giving a very full explanation, but he got out of Vancouver pretty fast. Am I correct that there are two in the office of northern affairs in Vancouver?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
And two in the post office?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is right.

In the examination the minister made of the Vancouver post office sub-office, would he tell us what he found there among the records, and also the same with northern affairs, because it is most unusual to have such a large staff just looking after general matters?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am tremendously surprised that the Leader of the Opposition raised that question because I thought of all the people in the committee he would not raise it. I must say I was surprised at finding the extent to which the B.C. people, including its business people, regard Ottawa as being-I do not want to use the term separated-a long

piece away, and the extent to which they go there for all manner and type of government information.
Are there no federal government offices in Vancouver?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, there are. I may say that right here in Ottawa I have found myself somewhat amazed at the extent to which I have found myself being interviewed by business and professional people in the whole of eastern Ontario about what they regard as eastern Ontario matters related to goven-ment business, and not of a political or party nature. This is a fact in this country. I have not yet gone over all the offices, but this is in the process of being done and if there are any abuses, action will be taken. I wish again to draw the attention of hon. members to that. I do not know what more I can say about this thing.
When I checked the one in Niagara Falls I began to wonder, in the light of some of the work there, what percentage of our total immigration had gone into that area. Frankly a lot of things rather surprised me. I was amazed to find the increased inquiries about immigration which were going into that office. I do not put this forward necessarily as a defence, but hon. members asked for information and I am giving them the information. I can only say this is being pursued right through. I did get around to the public works office in Montreal. I found that it has a smaller staff than is usual. The question raised there was whether these people were doing more than the minister's office work-whether they are doing work that should be done by the departmental staff, in which case we may have to add departmental staff there. There is a practice there of getting information about publicly called tenders, a practice which apparently has gone on in that province over a great number of years, no matter who is minister.

I am wondering whether these people are not doing some of the work we ourselves are supposed to be doing. Take the postal department; I have not had a letter from the postal department in my constituency for a year. When I was on the other side, I used to have many letters about vacancies coming forward, and so on-
Oh, oh.

It is no laughing matter. I am talking about legitimate business. When postal services are required in my area I think it is my duty to my constituents to

see that those situations are adequately filled. It is not a question of patronage. I think the reaction from the government side of the house is very unpleasant. I want to know why I am no longer asked to help supply adequate postal services throughout my district. As I say, I have not had a letter for a year. Where are they going?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Perhaps I can help the hon. member by reminding him that I, like himself, was a private member supporting a government for some years, and I was a private member of the opposition for some years. And I am not surprised at what he says.
I am.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That may be. What the hon. member says is undoubtedly true, but I do not know that it is germane to the point at issue here.
I think so. If you are spending $2,000 in any place in Canada on work which could be done by members here, I think it is not money well spent. This is a legitimate job-

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, it is not part of a member's job to perform the duties required of ministers of the crown. It is the duty of the hon. member to discharge his obligations as a member of the House of Commons and of the parliament of Canada. What we are discussing here is whether or not these employees are performing the duties of a minister of the crown.

I did not get a list of all the
various ministers who have representatives, ambassadors or assistants in their constituencies or other places.
None in Alberta.

I was thinking in terms of one of the ministers, the Postmaster General who, before being offered that important portfolio, was minister of forestry. I would be interested to know what is the position in cases of this kind, where the duties of a minister are changed. What happens with regard to the assistants in these cases. For example, what happened to the assistants credited to the minister of forestry in Vancouver? Were any new orders in council passed to deal with the situation when the minister became Postmaster General? Did they become attached to him in his new capacity? I think this is a point of some interest.
Interim Supply

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would want to check that before giving an answer because I do not know exactly what the procedure is. In any event, the two employees in question are on the minister's staff now, attached to the Postmaster General; they were on his staff formerly, when he was minister of forestry. However, I would want to check the technical aspect of the question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not wish to participate in the discussion this afternoon, but the President of the Privy Council I think suffered a lapse from his usual standard of veracity when, in answer to an interruption of mine, he cast doubt on my truthfulness. He was talking about ministerial assistants in the province of Manitoba, in the office there, and I said "But no ministerial assistants in the office". He said "When you check Hansard you may wish to revise that statement". I do not wish to do so at all. Never, when I was a minister of the crown, did I have a ministerial assistant appointed outside the city of Ottawa, and I hope the President of the Privy Council will, in fairness, correct the inference to the contrary which he left on the record.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, I am happy to correct it. The hon. member-and I think Hansard will support me in this-says "in that province". He said "no one in that province", and I looked directly at the minister concerned. There was an employee of the minister's staff, as he knows, in that province. The hon. gentleman is quite correct as far as I know. He did not have any employee of his minister's staff in the province.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I wrote down what I said, and the words I used were "in that office". I hope that my correction when I interrupted the Minister of Veterans Affairs is correctly shown, too. He said that all his predecessors had personal assistants in the office in Winnipeg as he has at the present time in St. Boniface. I attempted to correct him because I did not have a ministerial assistant serving in the office which was available in the city of Winnipeg; I had nobody on my staff serving outside Ottawa.
May I say, with regard to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, that the department has in the city of Winnipeg a very large office to which I always referred the problems of veterans which arose in Winnipeg and in Manitoba when I happened to be in the city of Winnipeg. Veterans would call me at the hotel and I would make sure that they were immediately looked after by the officials of

Interim Supply
the Department of Veterans Affairs. That is precisely what should be going on at the present time.

Perhaps I could throw a little light on this matter. It seems to me that the President of the Privy Council was looking in my direction when he referred to Manitoba. When I became a member of the treasury benches I was informed there was an office available in my constituency to which I was entitled to appoint a representative. This I did. However, it was not long until the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who all the time that I was minister of northern affairs and national resources performed the function of being the controller of the conscience of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, raised objections in the form of complaints, with the result that I decided it would be desirable, in the best interests of good administration to withdraw the representative from my local constituency office. I think the appointment was made in November, and it was withdrawn in February. From that point on the office was available. It was served by representatives of my staff here in Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member what year that was?
That was 1960-61.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, were the members of the hon. member's staff actually attending the office in Brandon?

No, not on a continuous basis. The office was there. I was informed by the Department of Public Works that the office was available in the post office building. I used it myself when I was in the constituency, and it was used from time to time by the secretarial staff in my office here in Ottawa.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask a question of the President of the Privy Council. If I heard correctly, the information given by the hon. member for Danforth was to the effect that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources has two appointees of a personal nature in Vancouver. Could I ask the President of the Privy Council to explain why there are appointees of northern affairs in that riding. I ask this question because I know the riding; Vancouver has been my home for 43 years. I would like to know if there are appointees of northern affairs in the riding of the minister; and if so, what is their job?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I dealt with both those questions earlier. I am not sure whether or not they are in the constituency. The building is the federal building at 326 Howe street, Vancouver. I believe it is not in the minister's constituency, but in any event it is in the city of Vancouver.

Are they two private appointees of the minister who are doing constituency work there? I should like to ask this question at the same time. I understand, also, that the Postmaster General has two such members on his staff, and I presume they are in the same constituency. What are the responsibilities of these four appointees?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I dealt with that matter a few minutes ago, Mr. Chairman. They are not employed on constituency affairs; that was the very point I made about them. They were ones I happened to have an opportunity to check, and they are not working on constituency affairs.
What are their responsibilities?
The minister has told us what they do not do. What do they do?

What are their responsibilities outside the offices of the Postmaster General and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources? These public buildings are in Vancouver Centre; there you have the complete staffs of northern affairs and national resources, and public works. What are the responsibilities of these four appointees over and above those of the normal staff?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They are on the ministers' staffs, as opposed to or distinct from departmental duties. That is a distinction I also tried to draw earlier in my remarks this afternoon. As a matter of fact, I differed a little with the leader of that party on that particular point, when he suggested that the duties in a minister's office should be performed by civil servants. I am sure he did not mean it to sound as it did, the way he put it.
Could I ask the hon. member, Mr. Chairman, whether he was in the chamber a few minutes ago when I gave this explanation?

Yes, I was. I think, Mr. Chairman, we have now come right down to it, in view of the statement of the President of the Privy Council, who has said that those four persons are not in these ministers' offices for departmental duties. Therefore, what are they? Are they party hacks?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman.
The minister, in his statement of about 30 seconds ago, said they are not there for ministerial or departmental duties.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not say they were not carrying out ministerial duties, Mr. Chairman. Surely the hon. member does not wish to put words in my mouth. I drew the distinction between ministerial duties and departmental duties. They are regular civil servants. This is a distinction I have always drawn in this house and, as a matter of fact, have fought a good deal about over the years. They are doing work that comes within the category of ministerial office duties, as distinct from those of the civil service. I also said they were not doing local party organization work or work of a party nature.

This is becoming somewhat ridiculous, sir. Is the President of the Privy Council saying there is a difference between ministerial and departmental duties? Is there such a difference, when the minister has a complete staff?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman; I am very firm in saying that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have one very brief question for the minister. Is there such an assistant in the constituency of the Minister of Transport, or is there just one for that whole province?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is none in that province, or for the Minister of Transport.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened very diligently to the remarks made this afternoon, and I think they are very important. I was interested in the last statement in particular, when the President of the Privy Council suggested that there is a difference between ministerial and departmental duties. This is not what the hon. member for Niagara Falls said when she explained the situation. She said-and I think this is exactly right and I do not think there is any doubt in the minds of hon. members about it- that she has a person in her riding doing the work of a member. It may well be, she said, that she receives a letter relating to welfare, which is a provincial matter, and is doing something that is really not within a member's responsibility; but I am sure it falls within the duties of every member of the house to handle matters that are allied to our job. I think we all do this-and these are the duties of a member of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
What about your secretaries?
Interim Supply

We certainly do not have secretaries who are able to do this type of work in our ridings. We do this as members of parliament. I certainly do not ask my secretary to do the job I am supposed to do as a member of parliament. But really this is what the Minister of National Health and Welfare was saying; that in her area she has someone to do the work that she had not time to do because her duties as minister take her into another field. Yet the President of the Privy Council is suggesting this is not the field; that the field is a limited one. It may be I am not familiar with the difference between the duties of a minister as minister of the crown and the duties of a minister as head of a department of government. There may be some fine distinction there. But the argument does not hinge on that; it hinges on whether the Minister of National Health and Welfare is doing the job to which the President of the Privy Council has referred, namely in the field of ministerial responsibility. Has the President of the Privy Council looked into the matter as to whether or not the Minister of National Health and Welfare, or for that matter the ministers of veterans affairs, northern affairs, fisheries and many others, have ministerial offices legally in their own areas to handle matters which as members of parliament they must handle? This is a highly technical question, because the act specifies that these people can only be appointed to a minister's office. Frankly, I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare did this, because she said earlier today that she had a brass nameplate on the door indicating to all and sundry that it was the office of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Not brass.

Well, the material does not matter, but the implication is that this office is an extension of her Ottawa office and should therefore be handling matters which I doubt whether the person she has in her office is capable of handling. I do not say that in disrespect to the person concerned, but the problems which come to a minister's office I would presume often need the advice and co-operation of the deputy minister concerned, or the advice of various heads of the department, because people coming to that office would not be asking about welfare or compensation matters but about matters which can only be settled by the staff in Ottawa.
I submit we are talking of two different things. I think the minister of health told

Interim Supply
us forthrightly and honestly exactly what her office was. If this was out in the open in my area you would not need to pay persons who are defeated candidates-because this is a patronage machine. I think there may be a role yet in politics for this. It has not been eliminated so far. If it has, it comes in conflict with the decision of the President of the Privy Council. My experience with the office of the privy council is that the minister goes into great detail and examines the matter very carefully, and I would be happy to have him take the whole matter under advisement.
There are two legal problems. One is whether or not the minister has the right to move her office around the country, which is something like the situation with the president of the United States. Is the president of the United States a guy who goes out and lays a cornerstone, or is he the guy who acts in an executive function? Books have been written on the division of these two responsibilities. In this case we will have to look at the office of the minister and at the work of the office of the minister to see whether the duty is performed in that sense.
I did not get much of a story from the Minister of Veterans Affairs and I do not know what is the function of the person in his office. It appears that he would rather have his office in St. Boniface than in Winnipeg, which raises a different question entirely. The minister of health and welfare made it clear enough that the President of the Privy Council will have to decide whether or not this office can be moved around.
Second, what is the function of the persons concerned? The act says that the minister may appoint his executive assistant and private secretary. This is done in a non-civil service way, and they act as the persons directly responsible in a political way. These people are always political people; they must be politically oriented or they would make a real botch of the problems which come to all of us here. Then the act goes on:
-and other persons to be employed in the office of a minister shall be appointed by the governor in council.
I think it is these others we are concerned with.
The only reason we are concerned in this matter is that it completely changes the aspect of government. If I am a poor member and very stupid I may have to hire someone to do my business in my constituency. As one hon. member has said, give me $5,000 to

stay at home and I will represent my riding better there than in Ottawa; and maybe that is true. But the question is whether or not we want to change the system which has existed for a long time and now put into ridings people who are paid a salary by the treasury board to look after our business. I think the President of the Privy Council will simply have to face up to the problem of whether I in Timiskaming, should have an executive assistant to handle the political business of Timiskaming, because I too have to be in Ottawa eight to ten months of the year. If such a person is supplied for a minister I suggest he should also be supplied for members. I think whether we should move the office of the minister from place to place is the crux of the problem, and that the President of the Privy Council should give us the legal opinion he receives on this. I suggest that he get the legal opinion, not necessarily from justice but from the law officers of the house, who have the right to make a report to parliament rather than just to a minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

I would only suggest, Mr. Chairman, that I would be quite happy to let it carry tonight if the minister will give me the assurance he will consider these matters, which will be important to members of parliament for many years to come.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes; I not only give that assurance but, as I have said, I am considering the matter now. In fact, the Prime Minister has instructed treasury board to do this, and that is on the record in Hansard.

Mr. Chairman, as far as I am concerned-and I speak now on behalf of the house leader-we are perfectly prepared to have the resolution carry now, on the undertaking that we will go ahead with the bill on Monday and with the committee stage of the bill. Frankly, I have some matters I want to comment on, as have other members. We will have the right on clause 1, as we do on any general bill, to have a general discussion in committee. If that undertaking is given and it is agreed we have a general discussion on the first clause, I think we could advance this resolution one stage tonight and carry on on Monday.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We are, of course, ready to give that undertaking.

We are happy to have the resolution pass, but over the week end would the

President of the Privy Council look up the legal opinion he received and table it in the house?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. As I indicated earlier I would not be prepared to table it. This has never been the practice in the House of Commons and there is a long argument on this which I will not enter into. But that has always been the position.
Is it not legal to get the legal officers of the House of Commons to give this kind of opinion?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think the practice is to get it from the attorney general. As far as I know that is the practice, and I am going back over a number of years. That is the responsibility of the Department of Justice.

I am sure that the President of the Privy Council is right when he says there has never been the tabling of an opinion in this house; but if parliament requests it I think there is a practice we could follow, which has been followed on several occasions in the past. The Minister of Justice could write to the President of the Privy Council saying that he cannot give the ruling that parliament has requested, but advise him in general terms, which really comes to the same thing. You get away from the tabling of a written opinion which, because I had to go into this one time myself, has never been done under the rules of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is a correct statement of the practice and we are quite prepared to follow it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The reason for this, of course, is that only the Attorney General of Canada or Minister of Justice has the responsibility of advising the crown, and any opinion from an officer of the law department is a draft opinion with which the Minister of Justice, under his responsibility, will or will not agree. The minister is the only one who has final responsibility, for such advice.
